Cybersecurity risk

Risk category
Operational
ESG factors
Social (S4)

Risk description:

Key mitigations:

The risk is related to geopolitical issues, which make the Group's key
services major targets for cyberattacks. The following vulnerabilities could
be exploited:

– periodically preparing and submitting vulnerability reports to responsible personnel;

– unresolved vulnerabilities in IT and OT systems;

– limiting and isolating critical systems within a local network;

– human factors, such as insufficient employee resistance to social
engineering attacks;
– inadequate privileged access control and monitoring of privileged users.

– implementing a vulnerability management process that classifies and addresses vulnerabilities based on their
criticality;
– developing digital security competencies by developing accredited CERT members in the organisation and
participating in cybersecurity exercises with external partners;
– ensuring 24/7 Group-wide cybersecurity supervision;
– maintaining an incident management process to ensure effective response;
– conducting regular phishing simulations across all Group companies to increase the vigilance of employees.

Compliance with financial
market transparency rules
The Group strives for maximum transparency,
effective management of inside information
and equality of all financial market participants
regarding the availability of the issuer's material
information. Effective prevention of market abuse
is one of our main priorities. The Group is listed in
both London and Nasdaq Vilnius stock exchanges
and complies with all relevant EU, Lithuanian and
UK laws and regulations.

Also, the Inside Information Disclosure Committee
(comprising 5 experts from finance, law,
compliance, investor relations and communication
areas) is operating successfully while dealing
with complex inside information management
issues and ensuring maximum transparency. In
its activities, the committee follows the principles
of ensuring proper competencies, managing
emerging risks, promptly making appropriate
decisions, constantly improving the knowledge of
the Group employees in the field of market abuse
prevention and implementing the best practices.

– updating the Trading Guidelines for the Issuer’s
Managers and Persons Closely Associated
with them, including the requirements and
prohibitions for issuer’s managers and persons
closely associated with them;

The Group is implementing Article 19 of the Market
Abuse Regulation (EU) No 596/2014 (MAR)
and applying a stricter Closed Period than the
requirements of Lithuanian and UK legal acts,
prohibiting trading for a period of 30 calendar
days not only before the publication of annual
and half-year financial results, but also before
the publication of three- and nine-month results,
including two days after their publication. In order
to ensure uniform disclosure of information on
managers' transactions in EU and UK markets,
the Group publicly discloses transactions whose
value exceeds EUR 5,000 during a calendar year
(in EU markets, transactions worth EUR 20,000
or more should be disclosed). Our goal is to
ensure even greater market abuse prevention and
transparency.

– updating the Group's inside information matrix
and periodically presenting specialized inside
information management instructions for target
groups;

In 2025, same as in the previous years, the Group
has successfully ensured the compliance with all
MAR requirements.

The Group's own internal market abuse prevention
and transparency rules are regularly updated,
and the main regulations are made available
to the public. The Group periodically trains its
employees on market abuse and insider rules.
The coordination of market abuse prevention is
one of the responsibilities of the Group Law and
Compliance.
The main market abuse prevention projects
carried out in 2025 include:

– introducing a new specialised inside information
management and share trading course to
those on the Insider List and to other Group
employees, which included material on inside
information management, trading securities,
market manipulation and closed periods.

Related party transactions
The parent company follows the provisions
of the Law on Companies of the Republic of
Lithuania(link in Lithuanian) when conducting
related party transactions. The Policy on Related
Party Transactions of the Group was updated by
the decision of the Supervisory Board on 16 June
2023 in accordance with changes in the provisions
of the Law on Companies of the Republic of
Lithuania. It must be noted that the Supervisory
Board of the parent company considers the
conclusions of the Audit Committee and makes
decisions regarding related party transactions of
the parent company and the Group companies
if these transactions meet all of the following
materiality criteria: (i) the type of the transaction is
an investment, acquisition, transfer, lease, pledge
and mortgage of assets, surety or guarantee for
the fulfilment of obligations; (ii) the amount of
the transaction or the aggregate amount of such
transactions during the financial year exceeds
1/10 of the asset value shown in the most recent
balance sheet; (iii) transactions are conducted
under unusual market conditions and/or are
not attributable to ordinary economic activities.
We disclose information about the concluded
related party transactions on our website and,
in accordance with the IFRS requirements, in
the section ‘8 Consolidated financial statements'
of this report. Additionally, according to Article
372(11) of the Law on Companies of the Republic
of Lithuania, the Group's management report
must include transactions concluded with related
parties regarding the investment, acquisition,
transfer, lease, pledge and mortgage of assets,
surety or guarantee for the fulfilment of obligations,
which are entered into in the ordinary course of
business under normal market conditions where
a transaction or the aggregate amount of such
transactions during the financial year exceeds

1/10 of the asset value shown in the most recent
balance sheet, as well as information on the legal
name, registration code, business form, official
register and address of the related party and the
amount of the transaction, which is also disclosed
in section ‘8 Consolidated financial statements’ of
this report.

5.1 Remuneration overview
Overview
Remuneration structure of the Group is based on
two key documents: the Remuneration Policy and
the Remuneration Guidelines. The Remuneration
Policy, which is a public document, defines
the key principles and essential provisions on
remuneration management and structure whereas
Remuneration Guidelines, which is an internal
document, is a supporting document detailing
the provisions of the Remuneration Policy (e.g.,
setting and evaluating objectives, determining and
paying short-term incentives). Both documents are
integrated and apply to all Group companies.
The overall objective of the Group Remuneration
Policy is to attract and retain competent, fastlearning, technologically advanced, globallyminded and creative employees. It includes
remuneration elements that support our strategy.
The Group is rapidly moving towards sustainability,
including the management of human resources.
Hence, the ongoing transition requires new
skills and competencies as well as continuous
development of our culture. In 2025, we continued
to develop our Remuneration Policy to maintain
the principles of transparency and clarity.

The Remuneration Policy’s approval process is
based on the Lithuanian Labour Code, the Law on
Companies and the Corporate Governance Code
for the Companies Listed on Nasdaq. The parent
company is required to submit any proposed
amendments to the Remuneration Policy for the
approval of the General Meeting of Shareholders.
We also inform and consult the representatives of
employees of the parent company and the Group
companies as well as other stakeholders about
changes to the Remuneration Policy (if any).
The latest version of the Remuneration Policy was
approved by the General Meeting on 7 May 2025
with 76.64% of the votes in favour (resolutions and
voting results) and is available on our website. To
ensure adherence to best governance practices,
the following changes have been in effect since 25
October 2025:
– the remuneration framework for the Supervisory
Board was reviewed and updated in preparation
for the new term. The revised structure
reflects the parent company’s commitment
to maintaining a competitive and transparent
remuneration model that aligns with market
practices, regulatory expectations, and the
scope of responsibilities of Supervisory Board
members.

Key activities in 2025
The Annual General Meeting of Shareholders
of the parent company held on 26 March 2025
agreed to the parent company's Remuneration
report for 2024, as part of the parent company's
Integrated Annual Report 2024. 99,99% of
shareholders, who participated in the vote, voted
in favor, and the decision was adopted accordingly
(resolutions and voting results). No remarks were
made regarding the document during the meeting.
Nevertheless, the parent company has considered
the observations provided by proxy advisory.
The Group also launched a number of additional
initiatives related to the changes in the Group’s
economic and work/social environment, such as:
– continuing to enhance the semi-flexible benefits
system by providing an increased variety of
options to choose as additional benefits and by
increasing the value of the benefits provided in
response to the market situation;

– continuing to apply a hybrid work model
by offering employees work flexibility, thus
improving their work-life balance. Our hybrid
work model allows employees to work 2 days
per week remotely. Additionally, we are offering
an opportunity to work from Lithuania, any other
European Union and selected other countries
for 2 consecutive weeks per calendar year.

Plans for 2026
In 2026, the Group will continue strengthening
its remuneration and people practices. The key
focus areas for the upcoming year will include the
implementation of initiatives related to the Pay Gap
Directive, further enhancement of the performance
management framework, and actions aimed at
fostering a high-performing organisational culture.
These priorities will support greater transparency,
improved employee experience, and sustained
organisational effectiveness.

– the introduction of a renewed recognition
programme aligned with the updated
behavioural mindsets of the Group. The
programme is designed to strengthen a culture
of appreciation, reinforce desired behaviours,
and promote the values and competencies
expected across the organisation.

Integrated Annual Report 2025 / Remuneration

Remuneration Policy and its
structure
The key objective of our Remuneration Policy is to
support the Group’s pathway towards achieving its
goals through 5 key principles on the right side.
The Remuneration Policy defines the remuneration
structure, the fixed base salary (FBS) review
and determination process, the composition of
the maximum variable remuneration, related
guidelines, principals, etc.
Overall, our Remuneration Policy is designed to
attract, retain, and motivate employees to ensure
the achievement of the Group’s objectives by
creating a high performing organisational culture.
Thus, we aim to pay the median of the market
where the Group companies operate. Depending
on the competitive environment in a certain
country or the strategic objectives set for a Group
company, a different remuneration ratio (higher
or lower) than the median of the remuneration
market may be set. To ensure the principle of
external competitiveness, the FBS salary ranges
may be determined and reviewed annually while

considering the data of an independent national
salary survey and the remuneration market trends.
Salary ranges are determined for each job level
based on the median of the salary market.
Due to the Group’s scale and organisational
complexity, locally available remuneration surveys
offer limited benchmark data for comparable
top management positions. For this reason, the
Supervisory Board was advised by an international
remuneration consultant who provides
independent opinion on executive’s remuneration
compared to the local salary market.
The remuneration structure is consistent
across the Group. It includes fixed and variable
remuneration parts, which are described in
detail in the following table. Additionally, further
information on short-term incentives (STI) and
long-term incentives (LTI) is provided separately in
the following pages.

Key principles of the Remuneration Policy
Internal fairness

We ensure that similar- or same-value-creating work is compensated
equally throughout the organisation.

External competitiveness

Employees are entitled to receive a competitive salary based on their
function, market conditions and geography.

Clarity

We aim that all employees are informed about how their performance,
competencies and qualification impact their remuneration package as
well as on what basis it is set.

Transparency

We believe in transparency and share our objective remuneration
criteria with our employees.

Equal opportunities and
non-discrimination

Decisions on remuneration must be made in accordance with
the provisions set out in the Remuneration Policy and the Equal
Opportunities and Diversity Policy in force in the Group.

The complete Remuneration Policy and People
and culture policy along with further information on
human resources management are available on
our website, and in the ‘6. Sustainability statement‘
under section ‘6.3 Social‘ of this report.

Short-term incentives

Long-term incentives

Short-term incentives (STI), i.e., a percentage of
the annual FBS paid to a particular position or
an employee for meeting the objectives set for
him/her, are cash-based and tied to performance
results. Objectives linked to STI usually support
the achievement of long-term objectives, which
incorporate financial targets, strategic projects and
key milestones, as well as sustainability results.

Following the IPO, the parent company provides
long-term incentives (cash-based) to align
with shareholders' expectations, retain key
executives, enhance their motivation, and
connect compensation to the long-term strategy.
These incentives are tied to the Group’s fouryear strategic plan and are linked to long-term
targets, which incorporate financial targets,
strategic projects and key milestones, as well as
sustainability results.

The maximum STI level, depending on the
employee’s position within the Group, is provided
in the following table. Additionally, further
information about STI objectives of members
of the parent company’s Management Board,
including the CEO, and the performance results
are provided in section ‘Remuneration of the
parent company’s Management Board’ below.
The minimum threshold for the achievement of
a specific objective is 70%, and if the objective
is achieved at a lower percentage, the objective
shall be considered as not achieved (0 (zero)
percent). Overachievement of the objectives is not
rewarded (except for sales positions where it may
be compensated; however, a cap on the maximum
bonus amount is applied). Deferral or recovery
of STIs are not possible in the Group. However,
it is possible to withhold their payment, reduce or
request to return the STIs in part or in full to/from
an employee who commits unlawful acts whilst
achieving the set objectives or in cases such as
the restatement of accounts or the submission of
erroneous data. Further details on this matter are
described in the Remuneration Policy (malus and
claw-back).

TSR (Total Shareholders Return) is calculated as the ratio of the difference between the average share price at the end of the period and the beginning of the period and adding the amount of dividends per
share over performance period to the share price at the beginning of the performance period. The average TSR (Total Shareholders Return) of Ignitis Group and EURO STOXX® Utilities Index is calculated
in the two-month period (Nov and Dec accordingly) preceding the beginning and the end of the performance period (January 1, 2022–December 31, 2025), in order to neutralize any possible volatility on the
market. TSR of Ignitis Group is calculated with the assumption that dividends are reinvested as well as EURO STOXX® Utilities Index used for benchmarking (based on gross return index type and EUR
currency). Change in the value of the Ignitis Group shares between the beginning and the end of the reference period calculated as a weighted average of the IGN1L (Nasdaq Baltic) and IGN GDR (London
Stock Exchange) prices based on volume traded. 2 Target will be measured according to the achievement scale with linear interpolation between the entry (70%) and target (100%) thresholds. 3 ROCE is
calculated by dividing Ignitis Group adjusted earnings before interest and tax (adjusted EBIT) by its capital employed (average net debt at the beginning and end of the reporting period + average book value of
equity at the beginning and end of the reporting period). 4 Gross installed capacity (COD reached), 2025. 5 Electricity SAIFI (System Average Interruption Frequency Index) is calculated based on the National
Energy Regulatory Council methodology, excluding (1) interruptions due to natural phenomena corresponding to the values of natural, catastrophic meteorological and hydrological phenomena indicators; (2)
interruptions due to failures in the network of the transmission system operator. Target objective is defined based on the decision of the National Energy Regulatory Council on January 26 of 2022
no. O3E-79. 6 Interruptions per customer is calculated in accordance with the methodology and principles applied in the period of setting the performance objectives excluding interruptions due to natural
phenomena corresponding to the values of natural, catastrophic meteorological and hydrological phenomena indicators when wind speed is ≥28 m/s and applied country level. 7 Cost inflation (For the specified
type of expenditure, considering the economic development scenario, eliminating one-off costs) minus 1-1.5 pp according to the National Energy Regulatory Council methodology. 8 Networks OPEX reduction
in real terms of 8.6 EURm over the four years 2022-2025 is calculated by eliminating the following one-offs according to the National Energy Regulatory Council methodology and additional exception for
Donation to Ukraine (125.3 EURm over the period): (1) One-offs according to the National Energy Regulatory Council methodology: (1.1) All one-offs submitted to and accepted by NERC are eliminated (84%
of all one-offs, or 104.9 EURm). (1.2) All NERC one-offs submitted and awaiting verification are eliminated (15% of all one-offs, or 19.1 EURm), based on historical precedent of approval for similar expenditure
categories. Verification is scheduled for 2026-10-15. (2) Donation to Ukraine (1% of all one-offs, or 1.3 EURm). 9 Based on the Ignitis Group GHG emissions level in 2020: 5.37m t CO2-eq. 10 Achievement of
target is assessed according to the methodology used to set the 2020 base for SBTi targets and the results concerning the Group's CO2 emissions in 2025 has been adjusted to take into account the material
effects that were not in the control of the Group: (1) The effects of electricity emission factors changes (2025 vs. 2020) are eliminated (emission factors used at the level of 2020); (2) GHG emissions related
to Vilnius CHP are eliminated, as it was not fully operational in 2020 (also eliminated from 2020 base); (3) GHG emissions accounting improvement adopted post 2020 are eliminated; (4) Regulatory related
material one-offs (TSO initiated must-run operations) are eliminated.

Integrated Annual Report 2025 / Remuneration

Handling STIs and LTIs in the event of
termination
In the event of termination of the employment
relationship, ‘good leaver’ and ‘bad leaver’
conditions are applied when paying STIs and
LTIs. The payment of STIs and LTIs is reduced
proportionately according to the time worked in the
position during the implementation period of these
objectives.
An additional condition for paying for the
achievement of STI objectives, in the event
of termination of the employment relationship
before the end of the reporting period, specifies
that intermediate STI results must be approved
by the appointing body. If the achievement of
STI objectives cannot be assessed because
the deadline for their implementation has not
yet expired, the most recent percentage of the
achievement of the objectives, which has been
approved or presented to the appointing body,
is taken into account in order to assess the
achievement of the above-mentioned objective
or, in the absence of such a percentage, the
achievement of the objective is considered to be
0 percent.
Overview of non-compete arrangements
Non-compete agreements with members of
the Management Board were concluded in
2023 together with an overall Non-Compete
Policy overview of the Group. According to the
Remuneration Policy, non-compete terms and
conditions for the CEO and the members of
the Management Board of the parent company
shall be determined by the Supervisory Board.
The Group’s Non-Compete Policy stipulates the
following standard non-compete agreement terms
and conditions applicable to the Group employees:

– 70% of the FBS as a monthly non-compete
compensation;
– 9-month non-competition period;
– non-compete conditions other than those
specified above are determined by a decision
of the parent company's Management Board
(except for the parent company's CEO and
members of the Management Board, for whom
all non-compete conditions are determined by
the Supervisory Board).
There were no non-compete payments made to
key executives in 2025.
Overview of the CEO’s contractual terms
Employment agreement is concluded between the
CEO and the parent company in accordance with
the Law on Companies. The CEO may resign by
a written notice addressed to the Management
Board that elected him. The Management Board
that elected the CEO decides on the removal
of the CEO within 15 days from the date of the
receipt of the resignation letter. Also, according to
the Law on Companies, the CEO may be removed
from office by the Management Board, taking
into consideration the opinion of the Supervisory
Board, without prior notice. A separate written
non-compete agreement was concluded with the
current CEO in accordance with the provisions of
the Labour Code on 1 March 2022. Non-compete
agreement conditions correspond to the Group’s
general and the best market practices.

Other information
1.	 The parent company’s Management Board
members may own shares of the parent
company, but shares are not granted as part of
remuneration by the Group. For further details
and the details on the trading guidelines for
the parent company’s executives and persons
closely associated with them, see section
‘4 Governance’ of this report.
2.	 None of the Management Board members
perform external consultancy work for the
Group.
3.	 There are no agreements concluded between
the parent company and the members of
the Management Board that provide for
compensation in case of their resignation or
dismissal without a reasonable cause or in
case of termination of their employment as a
result of the change in control of the parent
company.
4.	 The remuneration of the members of the parent
company's Management Board for participating
in the activities of the committees or collegial
bodies of the Group companies is included
in their remuneration for their activities in the
Management Board. The parent company’s
Management Board does not receive any
remuneration (e.g., board fees or similar) from
Group or associated companies in the Group.
5.	 No special benefits or payments that are not
required by the Labour Code or not mentioned
in remuneration structure (under ‘additional
benefits’ part) are provided to the members of
the Management Board of the parent company.

5.3 Remuneration of the Supervisory Board and committees
Overview
The remuneration principles for members of the
Supervisory Board and committees of the parent
company are established under the Guidelines
for the Corporate Governance of a State-Owned
Energy Group, the Description of the Procedure
for the Payment of Remuneration to Members of
the Collegial Bodies of State Owned Enterprises
and Municipal-Owned Enterprises, as approved
by Resolution No 794 of the Government of the
Republic of Lithuania of 3 August 2022 (link in
Lithuanian), and Remuneration Policy. Following
the recommendations of the Governance
Coordination Centre and the best market
practices, the principles of remuneration for the
members of the collegial bodies of the parent
company and the Group companies were adjusted
in 2025 by starting to pay the remuneration for
participation in the committees. This principle
came into force after the General Meeting
approval of the amended Remuneration Policy on
7 May 2025. We expect this change to improve
the remuneration transparency, clarity and
competitiveness.

Key principles of the remuneration of the
Supervisory Board and committees of the
parent company
The monthly remuneration paid for the activities
in the Supervisory Board and committees was
set according to the Guidelines for the Corporate
Governance of a State-Owned Energy Group
and best market practices. The Group has also
set other remuneration principles, including the
following:
– remuneration for the activities in the
Supervisory Board and committees does not
depend on the performance of the parent
company or the Group companies;
– remuneration for the activities in the
Supervisory Board and committees is fixed for
the full term and can be reviewed once during
the entire term of office but not earlier than in
the mid-term of a collegial body, during the
Annual General Meeting of Shareholders of the
parent company;
– remuneration of the members of the parent
company's Supervisory Board for participating
in the activities of committees is paid
additionally;
– members of the Supervisory Board and
committees are not entitled to severance
payments upon termination of their contractual
relationship.

Integrated Annual Report 2025 / Remuneration

Gender pay gap and pay ratio

Pay ratio

Gender pay gap

In line with our commitment to transparency and
fair remuneration practices, we disclose the pay
ratio between the total remuneration of the highest
paid employee in the Group and the median
annual compensation of all other employees. As
part of our broader ESG strategy, we strive to
maintain a reasonable and justifiable pay ratio.
Our aim is to ensure that compensation aligns with
company performance while prioritizing fair wages
and benefits for all employees.

In 2025, the overall gender pay gap within the
organisation was insignificant. These results
underscore our ongoing efforts to promote equity
and fairness in remuneration practices, ensuring
alignment with our organisational values.
However, larger discrepancies are observed
when analysing the pay gap across different
employee categories. The gender pay gap is
influenced by several factors, including the
distribution of roles by gender, differences in
years of experience, and the dominance of men
or women in certain sectors. The largest pay gaps
are observed at senior executive and workers
levels. We are committed to reducing this gap by
promoting gender equality within the organisation,
investing in talent management processes, and
implementing equal opportunity principles at every
stage of decision-making.
Average gap in pay was calculated based on the
average fixed and total remuneration using the
following formula:
(Average gross monthly fixed/total
remuneration of male employees – average
gross monthly fixed/total remuneration of
female employees) x 100

Sustainability overview
Sustainability performance in 2025
Greener and more efficient energy
Green Share of Generation amounted to
70.2% (11.3 pp lower YoY).

GHG emissions increased by 54.7% in

compared to 2024.

Carbon intensity of our Scope 1 & 2 GHG
emissions increases by 24.5% YoY to 248 g
CO2 eq/kWh due to a higher electricity
generation in Elektrėnai complex.

The total number of installed smart meters
exceeded 1.3 million. We have achieved
our goal of installing over 1.2 million smart
meters by 2026 and are continuing with
the programme

At the end of 2025, a total of 1,799 EV
charging points were installed (+708 YoY).

Employee satisfaction (eNPS) remained
high – 65.6 in 2025 (65.2 in 2024).

For the fifth year in a row, the Group was
awarded the international Top Employer
2026 Lithuania Certificate for applying the
highest HR management standards (after the
reporting period).

Well-being mentors presented teams with
a package of resilience-building activities.
These activities help to better understand
mutual interaction, refine team operating
principles, foster community, and strengthen
trust. They encourage the team to talk openly,
agree on rules for cooperation, and create a
healthier, resilience-supporting work culture.

18.8 hours per employee was devoted to
training in 2025 (21.3 hours per employee
in 2024).

Awarded 107 scholarships for students in

100% of the Group’s public and 90% of
commercial procurements1 were green (100%
of total completed procurements1 in 2025).

The Group received ‘A’ governance score
in Lithuania in the SOEs Good Corporate

the highest ‘A+’.

Integrated Annual Report 2025 / Sustainability statement

6.1 ESRS 2: General information
The Sustainability statement offers a
comprehensive overview of the Group’s
commitment to environmental performance,
social responsibility, and governance practices.
In the following statement, disclosures are based
on material impacts, risks and opportunities
identified during the double materiality
assessment. The statement is organised into five
sections:     
– general information (ESRS 2);
– environmental information (E1, E4, E5);
– social information (S1, S2, S3 and S4);
– governance information (G1);
– other information.

BP-1 General basis for preparation of
sustainability statements
The Sustainability statement is prepared in
accordance with the European Sustainability
Reporting Standards (ESRS), which were
transposed into the law of the Republic of
Lithuania on 1 July 2024 and supplement the
Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive
(CSRD). All the disclosures included in the E,
S, and G sections have either been assessed
as material according to our double materiality
assessment (DMA) or are mandatory according
to the ESRS.
This Sustainability statement has been prepared
on a consolidated basis while aligning with
the scope of the financial statements for 2025
and ensuring consistency and comprehensive
coverage of our operations and activities.
All subsidiaries of the Group are included in
this consolidated Sustainability statement and
are exempted from individual or consolidated
sustainability reporting pursuant to Articles 19a(9)
or 29a(8) of Directive 2013/34/EU.
The Sustainability statement covers the Group’s
own operations as well as both upstream and
downstream aspects of its value chain, including
suppliers, distribution, product use, and end-oflife considerations, where possible.

No information corresponding to intellectual
property, know-how or the results of innovation
has been omitted from the Sustainability
statement. Also, the exemption allowing the
omission of disclosure related to impending
developments or matters under negotiation has
not been applied.
BP-2 Disclosures in relation to specific
circumstances
No material changes were made in the
preparation and presentation of the Group’s
sustainability information compared to the
previous reporting period. Contextual changes or
updates are disclosed thematically and specified
in section ‘7.3 Notes on restated figures’. No
material errors were identified in the previous
reporting period.
The Sustainability statement follows the
categorisation of short-, medium- and long-term
time horizons depending on a particular matter
(for more, see IRO-1 of time horizons used in the
double materiality assessment and MDR-A for
time horizons used for actions). No data has been
estimated using indirect sources in metrics that
include value chain, unless otherwise stated in
the accounting policy for that data (e.g., for GHG
emissions). If new data has been introduced to
the disclosures based on ESRS requirements,
the comparative information is not provided for

such data point unless this data was previously
reported and comparative information is available
or can be easily accessed. Additionally, no
quantitative metric or monetary amount provided
has been identified that would be subject to a
high level of measurement uncertainty, unless
otherwise stated in the accounting policies or
alongside relevant disclosure points, where these
estimates are described (e.g. reporting year
OPEX for Green Capacities expansion projects in
paragraph ‘E1-3 Actions and resources in relation
to climate change policies’).
No external body, other than the assurance
provider, was involved in validating
the measurement of any metrics in the
Sustainability statement.
The Sustainability statement does not include
additional information required by other
legislation or sustainability reporting standards.
Cross-referencing within Sustainability statement
and incorporation by reference within the
management report is used to avoid duplication
of information.

GOV-5 Risk management and internal control
over sustainability reporting
The Group Sustainability function is tasked with
leading the development of comprehensive Group
reports on sustainability issues and Environment,
Social and Corporate Governance (ESG) metrics.
The Group Sustainability function works closely
with the Group Finance, Group People and
Culture, Group Health & Safety and Environment,
and other functions to organise and lead
essential activities for sustainability, including
the consolidated DMA, evaluating climate risks,
and managing data collection and conversion
processes for sustainability reporting.
The gathering of relevant data and information for
the Sustainability statement is a continuous effort.
The primary risks in creating unified sustainability
disclosures across multiple companies include
human errors and data misalignment. To minimise
reporting errors, the Group Sustainability function
oversees a unified sustainability-related data
framework for the entire Group and follows
a systematic risk prioritisation methodology.
This standardises definitions, calculations, and
critical metrics, such as the emission factors in
compliance with the GHG Protocol.

After the first reporting cycle in 2024, we
continued to enhance our reporting structure by
walking through existing processes, implementing
additional controls, if necessary, strengthening
internal sustainability team expertise and
implementing digitalisation solutions to make
reporting process standardised and convenient.
The Group is continuing its work on building
Sustainability DataHub to have consolidated
sustainability data in a central data platform.
A separate Sustainability Reporting division
that is responsible for preparing sustainability
disclosures under the CSRD has been
established in 2025.
All sustainability data is now based on the
principles outlined by the ESRS.

The Head of Group Sustainability regularly
informs the CEO and CFO about the progress of
the preparation of Sustainability statement.

SBM-1 Strategy, business model and
value chain
Sustainability is an integral part of the Group’s
strategy and, to achieve the goal to create a
100% green and secure energy ecosystem for
current and future generations, clear purposedriven priorities were set in the Group's strategy.
For more information on the Group’s strategy and
business model, see section ‘2.2 Strategy and
targets’.
Five strategic sustainability priorities with ESG
targets were set in our Strategic Plan 2025–2028,
focusing on: decarbonisation, safety, employee
experience, diversity, and sustainable value
creation. Together, these five areas respond to
the Group’s material sustainability impacts, risks,
and opportunities.
The Group creates value by developing green
generation and green flexibility projects,
generating energy from renewable and nonrenewable energy sources, distributing energy
and ensuring reliable energy supply throughout
Lithuania and offering sustainable products to
our customers. There are four strategic business
segments in the Group – Green Capacities,
Networks, Customers & Solutions, Reserve
Capacities. Each of them is essential to the
business model of the Group and create value to
the Group and its stakeholders.

Key inputs and our approach

Key outputs and created benefits

Materials

Customers

The Group depends on natural resources, like
wind, sun and water, to produce green energy,
as well as other critical resources (natural gas,
copper) to produce energy from non-renewable
sources, and to distribute and supply energy.

The Group delivers reliable energy access and
offers sustainable solutions to its customers. By
supporting businesses in meeting their energy
needs responsibly, the Group enables them
to adopt choices that are both efficient and
environmentally sustainable.

Human capital and financial resources
Human capital is essential for the operations
of the Group. Every day, the employees of the
Group apply their skills and expertise to build
long-term value, guided by the principles of
the Group. Financial resources are essential
to the business model of the Group, enabling
continuous investment and improvement across
the activities of the Group.

Communities
We create value for the communities where
Green Capacities’ projects are developed by
maintaining open communication and ongoing
dialogue. The Group works to ensure that local
residents benefit from these initiatives and
creates lasting positive outcomes that support the
communities.

Stakeholder relationships

Shareholders

The Group’s success relies on active dialogue
with its stakeholders, including government
bodies, environmental organisations,
shareholders and suppliers. The dialogue is
essential as, without it, the Group would not be
able to carry out its operations.

The Group offers an attractive blend of growth
and yield driven by an integrated business model
and financial discipline. This approach has
enabled Adjusted EBITDA to more than double
and dividends to grow steadily, both since the IPO
in 2020, supporting continued value creation for
shareholders.
Employees
We create safe and inclusive work environment
while providing our employees with opportunities
for career development and growth.

Integrated Annual Report 2025 / Sustainability statement

IRO-1 Materiality
assessment process

The Group recognises the importance of aligning
its business operations with the expectations of
its stakeholders and the broader environmental
and social landscape. Using the concept of
materiality, the Group can identify, prioritise, and
then manage the key topics of sustainability.
Following the implementation of CSRD and
ESRS, the Group is using DMA’s approach to see
both the extent to which the sustainability topics
impact the Group and the Group’s impact on
these topics.
The Group conducted its first DMA in 2024,
while applying the guidance available from the
European Financial Reporting Advisory Group
(EFRAG) combined with its experts’ interpretation
of the standards, and developed a step-by-step
process, scoring methodologies, and a model
for aggregation and prioritisation. In 2025, the
Group repeated the DMA exercise to update and
improve its processes and evaluate the results.
To conduct the DMA, the Group has built on its
previous experience of assessing the materiality
of sustainability-related matters. The starting
point was updating the value chain maps for all
four business segments and later following with
an impact assessment (inside-out) to gauge
what impacts on the environment and the society
the Group has. In parallel, the Group has also
conducted a financial assessment (outside-in) of
the sustainability-related risks and opportunities
the Group is exposed to. Where possible, the
Group quantified the effects of sustainabilityrelated risks and opportunities and supplemented
them with qualitative assessments. For DMA,
the Group used previously conducted climate
change scenario analysis, asset-level climate-

related risks assessments, consulted with
external environmental groups, conducted an
internal human rights impact assessment and
used other internal analysis / materials of different
topics. Then, following the internal assessment,
conducted by internal experts, including but
not limited to risk management, finance,
sustainability, HR, HSE and other professionals,
the Group defined the list of material IROs. The
list of material impacts was validated by internal
and external stakeholders, risks and opportunities
were validated internally and, later, the full list of
material IROs received an official agreement from
the parent company's Management Board.
For more information on how sustainability risks
are integrated into the overall risk management
process of the Group, see section '4.7 Risk
management'.
Although the Group is confident in the validity
of its findings, it must be acknowledged that the
methodology may not be without limitations.
Consequently, the Group will be further
developing and strengthening its DMA process
while corresponding to the simplification of ESRS
and making further updates.
Double materiality assessment methodology
(incl. process steps for both impact and
financial materiality)  
The Group has developed methodologies with
reference to the principles stated in the Annex
I of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU)
2023/2772 of 31 July 2023 and in the ESRS
implementation guidance of double materiality
by EFRAG.

Methodologies and assumptions  
Scope
The Group has identified and assessed the
impacts of its own operations on the people and
the environment as well as the potential business
risks and opportunities. Furthermore, the Group
assessed the IROs in its value chain in most
topics, focusing on what has arisen during value
chain mapping for different business segments.
The value chain assessments were based on
our internal knowledge and mainly focused
on the first-tier suppliers, while incorporating
a comprehensive coverage of the second tier,
where possible.
During the impact assessment, the Group
considered both positive and negative impacts
as well as actual and potential impacts related
to sustainability matters. This year we were
concentrating more on the negative impacts
as recommended after the first cycle of DMA
disclosures. During the financial assessment, the
Group assessed potential sustainability-related
risks that could trigger a significant negative
financial effect on its businesses. In the same
way, the Group assessed opportunities that
could trigger a significant positive financial effect.
The opportunities identified in this process were
directly connected to the Group’s strategy.
The Group developed a consolidated DMA
process that applies to the whole Group and is
conducted annually.

Stakeholder engagement

Scoring of impacts  

Scoring of risks and opportunities

Process

Internal subject-matter experts from the Group
companies and the Group functions were
involved in the DMA, and a dedicated team
was established to coordinate the process
with sub-teams deployed to assess the impact
and financials.

As per the ESRS guidance, impact materiality is
calculated by multiplying the severity of impacts
by their likelihood. The average of the parameters
of scale, scope, and irremediable character
have been used when scoring the severity of
impacts. Scorecards were developed based on
the following methods of calculating different
parameters of impact:

Same as with impact materiality, following the
ESRS guidance, the financial materiality of risks
and opportunities was calculated by multiplying
the likelihood of occurrence by the financial effect.
When assessing the potential financial effect,
both quantitative and qualitative approaches were
used. The quantitative approach used profitability
(Adjusted EBITDA, net profit) as the key financial
parameter. Additionally, the qualitative approach
was used where effects could not be reliably
measured in financial terms or additional effects
had to be assessed, and the scoring was based on
expert judgement.

The Group has defined process phases for
conducting the DMA for impact materiality and
financial materiality, respectively. The impact
assessment was the starting point, followed by
the financial assessment. The process focused on
the Group’s business segments and IROs found
in their value chains. No exclusion or heightening
of specific activities, geographies or business
relationships used. The Group followed the six key
phases presented below:

As mentioned above, direct dialogue with the
affected stakeholders about the impacts the
Group may have or has through its business
activities has been included in the DMA, with
some in identification stage and with all as
a form of validation of internal results. The
results of the assessment of material IROs
present a consolidated view of what the Group
has assessed internally and how these results
were validated by the stakeholders. The parent
company’s Management Board has been
informed of the results of the dialogue with
stakeholders and their views on material impacts.
Time horizons
In its double materiality assessment, the Group
follows the categorisation of short-, medium- and
long-term time horizons as defined in ESRS
1(6.4.) and according to the Group’s Strategic
Plan, corresponding to:

– when scoring scale, the Group assessed how

grave or beneficial the impact is or could be for
the environment or society;

– when scoring scope, the Group assessed how

widespread the impact is or could be;  

– when scoring irremediable character, the Group

Thresholds  

– when scoring likelihood, the Group assessed

For both impact materiality and financial
materiality, the same quantitative
threshold was used as in the Group Risk
Management Framework.

assessed how hard it is to counteract or remedy
the resulting harm;
the chance of the potential impact happening,
and for actual impact the maximum score was
given.

– engaging stakeholders;  
– mapping detailed value chains;
– listing and grouping IROs;
– impact and financial assessments;
– validating material IROs;
– determining final material IROs.

For negative impacts specific scorecards have
been developed to prioritize them.

– short-term – up to 1 year (corresponding to

2025);

– medium-term – 2 to 4 years (corresponding to

2026–2028);

– long-term – 5 years and more (corresponding to

2029 and further).

Corresponding years have not changed since last
year as they are now aligned with the Group’s
Strategic Plan.

Process phases
Impact materiality
The work on mapping sustainability-related
impacts draws on our previous experience, along
with the latest studies, dialogue and internal
projects.
1. Engaging stakeholders

After ten topical ESRS were analysed, subjectmatter experts within the Group’s companies
and Group functions who have knowledge in
these areas and a strong understanding of a
day-to-day work of the Group were identified.
Through several onboarding sessions, the
Group developed a shared understanding
of the new regulation, the objectives of the
double materiality assessment, and stages
that would follow to conduct the assessment.
The map of internal stakeholders to be
involved in the DMA has been developed.

2. Mapping value chains

Internal subject-matter experts within the
Group’s companies were engaged to update
the value chain maps of business segments.
This stage included understanding how
diverse value chains look like in different
business segments, what impacts they have in
different parts of the value chain.

3. Listing and grouping impacts

After value chains were mapped, the
extensive lists of identified actual and potential
impacts were prepared. These impacts were
grouped as per ESRS and merged in cases
of recurrence; thus, the list of the Group’s
impacts was prepared.

4. Impact assessment

The Group conducted several impact
materiality assessment workshops to assess
the summarized list of impacts. Participants
adjusted the pre-defined impacts where
relevant and added additional impacts, then
scored all impacts within the Group’s own
operations and the value chain according to
the developed impact scoring methodology
and scorecards. Scoring assumptions
were documented, and relevant reference
documents were captured. All input from
workshops was transferred to a DMA tool to
aggregate scores and calculate the materiality
level.

5. Validating material impacts

The list of material impacts that passed the
materiality level threshold was presented and
discussed with stakeholders via dialogue,
where the Group asked to rate how important
the Group's impact (including through
business relationships) on the environment
and/or people is to them in relation to the
sustainability themes. In addition, this year
stakeholders were asked to identify, which of
the impacts they perceive themselves.

6. Determining final material impacts

The consolidation of internal impact
assessment and validation results allowed
us to finalize the list of material impacts. The
finalised list of material impacts was presented
to the Supervisory Board and later agreed
upon by the parent company’s Management
Board.

Financial materiality
Financial materiality assessment focused on
potential sustainability-related risks and potential
sustainability-related opportunities. Note that
the Group considers only financially material
sustainability risks that are incorporated and
disclosed along with enterprise Top risks covered
in the '4.7 Risk management' section.
1. Engaging stakeholders

The Group analysed the ten topical ESRS and
identified subject-matter experts within the
Group companies and Group functions who
have knowledge and a strong understanding
of the Group’s day-to-day work. The Group
also engaged relevant stakeholders to ensure
appropriate consideration of sustainabilityrelated risks. These included internal
subject-matter experts in the fields of risk
management, finance and sustainability, and
other experts when needed. A dedicated team
to conduct financial materiality assessment was
established with an oversight from the CFO.

2. Mapping value chains

Internal subject-matter experts within the
Group’s companies were engaged to update
the value chain maps of core business
segments. This stage included understanding
how different business segments value chains
look like and what risks and opportunities may
arise in different parts of the value chain.

3. Listing and grouping risks and opportunities

After the value chains were mapped,
an extensive list of identified risks and
opportunities was prepared. This process
reflects our approach last year, when a broad
assessment was conducted to capture a wide
range of potential risks and opportunities.
They were grouped according to the ESRS
and merged in cases of recurrence, resulting

in a consolidated list of the Group’s risks and
opportunities. Where possible, the risks were
also matched with the risks already identified
by the Group or its companies. This year, our
approach was more focused: the process
was built upon the previously developed and
analysed list, which was refined to reflect
the most recent updates and developments.
This allowed for a more targeted and
efficient identification of relevant risks and
opportunities, ensuring continuity while
integrating new insights.
4. Financial assessment

The dedicated team assessed the financial
materiality of the risks and opportunities based
on an established financial methodology and
scorecards. This year, its methodology was
further refined – especially the qualitative
part. Overall, the assessment became less
reliant on expert judgement and incorporated
a more structured reasoning and documented
justification. The team engaged extensively
with the Group companies through workshops,
etc., to gather the necessary information for
consolidation of the information.

5. Validating material risks and opportunities

The list of material risks and opportunities
that passed the materiality threshold was
presented and discussed with the parent
company’s Management Board.

6. Determining final material risks and

opportunities
The internal financial materiality assessment
was enhanced with inputs received during
validation session, which allowed us to finalise
the list of material risks and opportunities. The
finalised list of material risks and opportunities
was presented to the Supervisory Board and
later agreed upon by the parent company’s
Management Board.

The results were grouped by ESRS topical
standards, showing that E1, E4, S1, S2, S3
and S4 are material sustainability matters from
both impact and financial perspectives. The
environmental IROs the Group has within E1
and E4 are closely linked to its strategic goals
to deliver a build-out of green generation and
green flexibility technologies, while noting the
importance of the Networks segment in the
energy transition. The deployment of green
capacities mitigates climate impacts but also
requires significant amounts of natural resources
with indirect negative impacts on the climate and
the environment. All the activities of the Group
also affect people and societies around it, which
is reflected in the impacts and risks the Group
has within S1, S2, S3 and S4. The Group focuses
its efforts on leading the energy transition in a just
and inclusive way, including for people working
across its supply chains, and in a way that brings
benefits to local communities.
E5 and G1 are also material sustainability matters
from an impact perspective.
The main changes in material topics since last
year were the following: E4 became material from
both impact and financial perspective (previously
only impact material), and E5 from double

E2: Pollution is an important topic to the Group
as its operations have a negative impact on
the air from non-GHG emissions (as SOx, NOx
and particulate matter). However, this impact is
strictly regulated in all our assets, and the Group
takes all necessary actions and remain below the
established limits. The Group companies which
operate generation assets consistently ensure
full alignment with the applicable Best Available
Techniques requirements by regularly updating
and revising their Integrated Pollution Prevention
and Control Permit conditions. As required by
legislation, these permit conditions are reviewed
or updated whenever operational changes
occur, thus confirming continuous and compliant
implementation thereof. The impact of pollution
of soil and water is also considered, regularly
monitored, and managed with precautionary
actions. However, these impacts are not
considered material in any given reporting year.
Pollution related KPI and metrics can be found on
page 287.
E3: Water and marine resources is also
considered in the Group’s DMA process as an
important topic, considering that the Group owns
and operates hydropower plants and use water
withdrawals in other assets. All water withdrawals
and discharges used in electricity and heating
operations are regularly monitored and reported.
While water remains an important topic for the
Group, it is not considered material for this

By being embedded into the Group’s strategy and
one of the core drivers, sustainability strengthens
our resilience to material impacts and risks while
opening new opportunities in a changing world.
For more information on the Group’s strategy and
business model, see section ‘2.2 Strategy and
targets’.
The Group does not consider that the risks
and opportunities identified during the double
materiality assessment's process have a material
financial impact on the financial position, financial
performance and cash flows of the Group in the
current reporting period. In addition, none of the
identified material risks and opportunities are
expected to result in material adjustments to the
carrying amounts of assets and liabilities reported
in the consolidated financial statements within the
next year. For future periods, the Group has opted
to exercise the phase-in allowance to omit the
anticipated financial effects of material risks and
opportunities on its financial position, financial
performance, and cash flows over short, medium
and long term.

Material sustainability related IROs
The following tables list the sustainability related
IROs the Group has identified and assessed
as material as a result of its double materiality
assessment.
Each material ESRS topic is presented in the
following tables, with specified sub-topics that the
identified material impacts, risks or opportunities
relate to, e.g. climate change mitigation and
climate change adaptation.  
In addition, it is indicated in the tables whether
the impacts and risks are in the Group’s own
operations (OO) or in its value chain (VC), actual
or potential. The Group also discloses whether its
impacts are positive or negative.
More information on each IRO is included in
the topical sections. The management of their
impacts is also presented there. More information
on risks, including their management, is
presented in section '4.7 Risk management'.

The list of material IROs has been updated since
last year, with the main changes being:
– new risk of ‘Non-compliance with environmental

requirements’ (E4) was determined as material;

– risk of ‘Materials and components shortage’

(reported last year under E5) was determined
as not material this year and is therefore
not disclosed;

– new subtopic was identified in E5 after internal

analysis and consultation; thus, disclosures
were prepared under sub-topic ‘Waste’;

– new negative impact of ‘Demanding working

environment’ (S1) was identified and determined
as material;

– positive impact of ‘Ensuring fair working

environment and remuneration’ (reported last
year under S1) was eliminated from the impacts
lists and is not disclosed;

– positive impact of ‘Promoting gender balance’

(reported last year under S1) was converted to
the cause of this impact and became negative
impact of ‘Unequal gender distribution’ (S1);

– new negative impact of ‘Disturbance and

diminishing of living conditions during
constructions’ (S3) was determined as material;

– other targeted changes were made to the IROs

or other technical details of value chain.

to be more significant. In addition, only the

the implementation of actions or action plan

at the Group level, no additional disclosures

is only presented in the ‘E1 Climate change’
topical standard as the Group’s transition plan.
Other standards present actions taken within the

reporting year. While the following time horizons
were used for the action plan in order to link it
with the Group’s Strategic Plan:

– long-term – 2029 and onwards.

Integrated Annual Report 2025 / Sustainability statement

Identifying climate-related impacts, risks and
opportunities
Identifying and managing our climate-related
impacts, risks and opportunities is central to
both mitigating operational risk and to achieving
our strategic goals. The Group periodically
tests the resilience of its strategy and business
model against climate-related impacts, risks
and opportunities, drawing on multiple inputs,
including the climate scenario analysis (CSA)
conducted in 2023, the DMA in 2025, and
climate-related risk management processes.
For additional information, see 'ESRS 2 IRO-1
Materiality assessment process'.
Use of climate scenario analysis
The CSA conducted in 2023 identified the
following physical and transitional climate-related
risks and opportunities that could arise under
a high climate-impact (4°C warming) pathway
and a net-zero (<1.5°C warming) pathway in the
medium-term (2030) and long-term (2050):
– physical risks and opportunities: associated

with extreme weather events (acute) and longterm climate changes (chronic);

– transitional risks and opportunities:

associated with transitioning into lowcarbon economy. There are five categories
of transitional risks: policy, legal, market,
technology and reputational risks.

According to Intergovernmental Panel on Climate
Change (IPCC) data carbon prices are expected
to increase by ~1.7x by 2030 and 3x by 2050
under the 1.5°C scenario. This could lead to the
Group facing a risk of increasing costs for energy
and heat generated by the Elektrėnai Complex,
Kaunas CHP and Vilnius CHP plants.

Climate scenarios, assumptions and outcomes
Physical risks and
opportunities  

This scenario represents the most 'unprecedented' or 'worst-case' scenario
from a physical climate change perspective, assuming a future with limited
mitigation measures, ongoing emissions growth at current rates and a global
average temperature increase of 4ºC by the end of the century compared to
pre-industrial levels.  

The assessment was conducted in four stages,
involving a broad group of internal stakeholders
across all business segments, and was overseen
by the parent company’s Management Board:

Future climate-related hazards and risks include:  
– rising temperatures;  

Stage 1: Interviews with representatives from
different activities were conducted to review
the existing climate-related risks, discuss other
potential climate-related risks and assess
opportunities. The results of this stage were
a long list of all possible climate-related, both
physical and transitional, risks and opportunities.
Stage 2: This longlist was narrowed down
by selecting the climate-related risks and
opportunities that are/could be the most material
to the Group. The final list was discussed
and approved by the parent company's
Management Board.
Stage 3: Modelling of the selected risks and
opportunities was conducted based on different
climate change scenarios.
Stage 4: Results were evaluated, and future plans
were set. All assumptions and outcomes are
disclosed in table on the side.

High physical impact (4°C warming) or no mitigation scenario based on the
Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 5-8.5 of the 6th IPCC (Intergovernmental
Panel on Climate Change) Assessment report.

– changing rainfall patterns;  
– increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather.  
The assessment scope: almost 300 sites, including Kaunas HPP; Kruonis
PSHP; Elektrėnai Complex; Vilnius and Kaunas CHPs; solar and onshore wind
farms; individual wind turbines.  
Transitional risks and
opportunities  

Rapid transition (<1.5°C warming) or high-mitigation scenario: net-zero
scenario of the International Energy Agency was used where available; for
some risks and opportunities the analysis also drew on other net-zero aligned
sources to complement the findings, where additional data was needed.  
This scenario presents a pathway to effective climate mitigation, which sees
global energy sector GHG emissions reach net zero by 2050, while also taking
into consideration other sustainable development goals, such as universal
access to energy and air quality improvements. Future risks and opportunities
include:  
– more stringent climate policies and carbon pricing;  
– technology innovation to support the low-carbon transition;  
– changing consumer market demands.  
The assessment scope: all four business segments of the Group and all
scopes (total) GHG emissions of the Group.

The 2023 CSA identified:
– three physical climate risks and one physical

climate-related opportunity;

– two transitional climate-related risks and two

transitional climate-related opportunities.

In the 2025 DMA only one physical climate risk
(acute and chronic climate-related events),
one transitional climate risk (lack of support for
energy transition) and one transitional climate
opportunity (global and regional renewable
energy landscape) were identified as financially
material. More details on the CSA, including its
results, can be found in the Integrated Annual
Report 2024.
Business resilience in relation to climate change
Resilience to climate change impacts, risks and
opportunities is achieved through the Group’s
overarching corporate strategy, risk management
processes, and decarbonisation measures.
Climate-related opportunities are captured
through the Group’s Strategic Plan 2025-2028,
which prioritises growth in green generation
and green flexibility capacity and positions the
Group to capture value from the energy transition.
Resilience to climate-related impacts is supported
by our investments and activities to reduce
emissions across our operations and value
chain. For additional information see paragraph
‘E1-3 Actions and resources in relation to climate
change policies’.

Material climate-related risks are integrated into
the processes of the Group Risk Management,
ensuring ESG factors are subject to the same
identification, assessment, and management
processes as other business risks. In 2025, the
Group introduced a dedicated tool to enhance
asset-level climate risk assessment and support
EU Taxonomy reporting. The tool monitors
assets reported under the EU Taxonomy and
screens them against climate- and naturerelated risks, providing granular, location-specific
projections. Projections for physical risks are
based on three IPCC scenarios (SSP1-2.6,
SSP2-4.5, SSP5-8.5) across baseline, 2030, and
2050 time horizons. The outputs also support
double materiality assessment and enhance
sustainability disclosures, ensuring that climaterelated considerations are embedded into
strategic priorities, investment decisions, and
operational planning.
The Group’s material risk relating to extreme
weather events is addressed through more
broad measures to mitigate energy infrastructure
failure. For more information, see section
‘4.7 Risk management’. Reports on risks and
risk management suggestions are shared
with relevant employees, including Risk
management and Finance functions. The financial
statements are prepared in line with the climate
scenarios – this is detailed in note ‘4 Significant
accounting estimates and judgments used in the
preparation of the financial statements’ of section
‘8 Consolidated financial statements’.

The Group retains a high degree of flexibility in
order to adapt its strategy and business model
to climate-related developments in the short-,
medium-, and long-term. The Group ensures
continued access to affordable financing by
aligning with the EU Taxonomy and embedding
climate considerations into its investment cases.
This capacity to adapt, combined with a strong
customer base and a clear decarbonisation
pathway, supports the Group’s positioning
to manage risks, capture opportunities, and
continue to deliver on its purpose to create a
100% green and secure energy ecosystem for
current and future generations.

material IROs.

adapt quickly to changing climate, market, and
regulatory conditions.

– Green Capacities: committed to increasing

installed green generation and green flexibility
capacities to 4–5 GW by 2030. This is expected
to significantly reduce GHG emission intensity
from power generation;

– Networks: working to improve the efficiency

of electricity distribution networks, which
is expected to reduce energy losses and
emissions, as well as investing in new
technologies, such as smart grids, to enable
demand-side management and reduce
peak load;

The guidelines are an annex to the Group
Environmental Policy, which defines and
details Group’s approach to environmental
protection including climate mitigation and
adaptation.
The Group
Sustainability Policy
(available on our
website)

E1-3 Actions and resources in relation to
climate change policies

All Group

– Customers & Solutions: offering customers

a range of low-carbon energy products (EV
charging network, biomethane, remote solar
farms, use of green electricity) and services
(smart energy consultations) and developing
energy efficiency measures (solutions based on
smart meter data);

– Reserve Capacities: maintaining and prolonging

the lifecycle of Reserve Capacities to keep up
with legal and energy security requirements.

The Group requires all Group companies to
adhere to the principles stated in the climaterelated policies and carries out periodic
monitoring and oversight.
Each Group company conducts an annual review
of its decarbonisation measures and reports
to the Group on its progress and efficiency.
Implementation decisions are made during annual

The Group is currently prioritising direct
emissions reduction measures through
engineering and technological solutions. While
it has not yet developed any carbon removal
initiatives, including nature-based solutions, these
solutions may be considered in the future.
Key decarbonisation levers, objectives and
actions taken by the Group
To take advantage of material opportunities and
address material impacts and risks, the Group
employs the following key decarbonisation levers
to support the achievement of its targets:
– deploying green energy and green flexibility

technologies;

– promoting energy efficiency and reducing

consumption;

– using green energy;
– substituting products;
– promoting electrification;
– switching fuel;
– avoiding GHG emissions.

All climate change mitigation and adaptation
actions aimed at managing or adapting to
physical climate change risks are provided in the
table below ‘Key decarbonisation actions, targets

E1-4 Targets related to climate change
mitigation and/or adaptation
As a member of the United Nations’ Business
Ambition for 1.5 °C campaign, that ran from June
2019 to October 2021, the Group has committed
to support global efforts to achieve net-zero
emissions worldwide by 2050.
In line with this commitment, the Group has
set its own target to reduce total absolute GHG
emissions to achieve net-zero emissions by
2040–2050.
To strengthen its commitment the Group has set
its science based targets that were validated by
SBTi in 2021. In 2025, its near-term greenhouse
gas emission reduction targets were updated
and new long-term (net-zero) emission reduction
targets were validated and published. The Group
is pursuing net-zero GHG emissions across its
value chain by 2040.
The SBTi’s Target Validation Team has classified
the Group’s Scope 1 and 2 near-term target
ambition and has determined that it is in line with
the 1.5°C pathway. The Target Validation Team
has also evaluated the Group’s Scope 1, 2, and
3 long-term target ambition, and determined that
the long-term targets are aligned with the SBTi's
1.5° C mitigation pathways for reaching net-zero
by 2050 or sooner.

As part of our science-based decarbonisation
pathway, which includes both direct and indirect
GHG emissions from the Group’s operations,
the Group is dedicated to the following SBTivalidated targets:
Overall net-zero target (Validated by SBTi):
the Group is dedicated to pursuing net-zero
greenhouse gas emissions across its value chain
by 2040.
Near-term targets (2030):
– reducing Scope 1 GHG emissions from

electricity and heat generation by 86.6% per
kWh by 2030 from the 2023 base year1;

– reducing Scope 1 and 3 GHG emissions from

fuel and energy related activities covering all
electricity sold by 79.9% per kWh within the
same timeframe1;

– reducing all remaining absolute Scope 1

GHG emissions and absolute Scope 2 GHG
emissions by 42% within the same timeframe;

– reducing absolute Scope 3 GHG emissions from

use of sold products for sold and distributed
fossil fuels by 42% within the same timeframe;

– reducing absolute Scope 3 GHG emissions from

purchased goods and services and all remaining
emissions from fuel-and energy-related activities
by 42% within the same timeframe1.

More information is available on the SBTi website
and on the Group’s website.

1

The target boundary includes land-related emissions and removals from bioenergy feedstocks.

Long-term targets (2040):
– reducing Scope 1 GHG emissions from

electricity and heat generation by 91.5% per
kWh by 2040 from the 2023 base year1;

– reducing Scope 1 and 3 GHG emissions from

fuel and energy related activities covering all
electricity sold by 94.5% per kWh within the
same timeframe1;

– reducing all remaining absolute Scope 1

GHG emissions and absolute Scope 2 GHG
emissions by 90% within the same timeframe1;

– reducing absolute Scope 3 GHG emissions from

use of sold products for sold fossil fuels by 90%
within the same timeframe1;

– reducing absolute Scope 3 GHG emissions from

purchased goods and services and all remaining
emissions from fuel- and energy-related
activities by 90% within the same timeframe1.

Accounting policies
All targets and the progress are tracked
periodically. Strategic targets tracked each
quarter and all others at least yearly.
The target boundary revalidated in 2025 includes
biogenic emissions and covers at least 95% of
the Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions (marketbased), whereas Scope 3 targets include at least
two-thirds of all Scope 3 emissions as defined by
the SBTi criteria.
As per current SBTi guidelines, the Group does
not use carbon credits and does not currently
plan to rely on carbon credits to reach the
above-stated targets. Unless explicitly stated
otherwise, the targets and the GHG emissions
progress reported in section ‘E1-6 Gross Scopes
1, 2, 3 and total GHG emissions’ refer to gross
emissions. The Group has not yet developed an
approach to residual emissions/neutralisation of
remaining emissions in the net-zero scenario.
The Group is not aware of any quantified external
factors (such as temperature anomalies) that
might influence the comparability of the baseline
value against which the progress toward the
target is measured. Therefore, the Group uses
the 2023 baseline value as this was the baseline
revalidated by the SBTi. The 2020 baseline
still used for long-term targets set for 20252026. There were no significant changes in the
target boundary in the reporting year. The GHG
emissions methodology was not significantly
changed since the update in 2024. For more on
the methodology update see section ‘E1-6 Gross
Scopes 1, 2, 3 and total GHG emissions’. The
range of climate scenarios that were considered
and the decarbonisation levers chosen for target
achievement are discussed in detail in section
‘E1-3 Actions and resources in relation to climate
change policies’.
External stakeholders were not involved in the
emission target-setting process.

E1-6 Gross Scopes 1, 2, 3 and total GHG emissions

Accounting policies

Scope 1 emissions increased by 55% due to additional services at the Elektrėnai Complex, which raised natural gas consumption.
Scope 2 emissions decreased by 4%, driven mainly by lower electricity‑loss emissions.
Scope 3 emissions increased by 4% due to higher natural gas use at the Elektrėnai Complex and a higher share of natural gas attributed to Networks for
distribution-related emissions.

The Group’s carbon footprint calculations are
based on the Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol
and aligned with the ESRS requirements.
Specifically, the calculations follow the GHG
Protocol Corporate Accounting and Reporting
Standard and the Corporate Value Chain
(Scope 3) Accounting and Reporting Standard.
Emissions are calculated throughout the value
chain as per the standard. Emission factors for
calculations have been used from researchbased Life-Cycle Analyses (LCAs) sourced
from ecoinvent v3.11, the UK Department for
Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (DEFRA),
and other known and qualified emission
factor databases.

– C5 is calculated based on actual waste data

Scope 2 emissions include indirect GHG
emissions from the generation of power, heat, and
steam purchased and consumed by the Group.
Scope 2 emissions are primarily calculated
as the power volumes purchased multiplied
by specific emission factors. Location-based
emissions are calculated based on average
country-specific emission factors. Calculations
using market-based emission factors consider
renewable power purchased and assume that
regular power is delivered as residual power.
Contractual Instruments such as Power Purchase
Agreements and Guarantees of Origin are used
in market-based calculations and covers 96%
of total energy purchased and 86% of Scope 2
emissions.

– C6 is calculated based on mileage allowances

subcategories (C1-C15):
– C1 and C2 are categorised spend data

multiplied by relevant spend-category-specific
emission factors;

– C3 is calculated based on actual fuel

consumption and power sales to end customers
multiplied by relevant emission factors;

– C4 includes waste transport to CHP plants;

multiplied by relevant emission factors;
for employee travel;

– C7 is calculated based on estimates of the

distance travelled and travel type (e.g. car
or train);

– C8 is included in Scope 1 and Scope 2

emissions;

– C11 is calculated based on actual sales

of natural gas to both end customers and
wholesalers. The different types of natural gas
sold have specific upstream and downstream
emission factors;

– C13 is calculated to cover energy use in

alignment with the GHG Protocol’s guidance and
the Group’s strategy.

separately and not included in total GHG
emissions (according to ESRS requirements).

The Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852
(hereinafter – Taxonomy Regulation) establishes
a common classification system for sustainable
economic activities and provides common
language to describe what an environmentally
sustainable activity is. The key role of this
regulation is to help scale the sustainable
investments, provide companies, investors, and
policymakers with appropriate definitions for
economic activities which can be considered
as environmentally sustainable. The Group
supports the need to direct investments towards
sustainable projects and activities to reach the
objectives of the European Green Deal.
The Group has been applying the provisions of
Taxonomy Regulation since 2021, by disclosing

Alignment assessment
All Taxonomy-eligible activities of the Group
identified in the EU Taxonomy Delegated
Acts were analysed in determining substantial
contribution and do no significant harm (DNSH)
technical screening criteria (TSC). After
screening of Taxonomy-eligible activities, it was

noticed that most of the Group’s activities share
the same description in Annex I and II of the
Climate Delegated Acts, meaning that they can
be eligible for both mitigation and adaptation
objectives. The Group only assesses the climate
change mitigation objective as it is more relevant
for its activities at this moment.

Substantial contribution to climate change
mitigation
Activities 4.1, 4.3, 4.10, 7.3 (d), 7.4, 7.6 (a)
automatically fulfil the substantial contribution
criteria to climate change mitigation as the
Group operates them in the manner requested
by the criteria. Activity 4.5 meets substantial

contribution criteria as the life-cycle GHG
emissions from the generation of electricity
from hydropower are lower than 100g CO2e/
kWh. Activity 4.9 is part of the interconnected
European system, i.e., the interconnected control
areas of Member States, Norway, Switzerland
and the United Kingdom, and its subordinated
systems, meaning this activity of the Group meets

Climate change adaptation
