Accounting policies
Main principles
Our accounting methodology for calculating
the key performance indicators required to be
disclosed by the Taxonomy Regulation (KPI) is
based on the Group’s best interpretation of the
Taxonomy Disclosures Delegated Act and the
currently available guidelines from the European
Commission. With regards to the limited
industry specific guidance, the Group made
several assumptions to practically implement
the Taxonomy Regulation. With the new official
guidance from the European Commission or the
industry’s best practices, these assumptions
will be amended and disclosed accordingly,
if needed.
While the Taxonomy Regulation requires to
disclose the share of revenue, Taxonomy OPEX
and Taxonomy CAPEX KPIs that are Taxonomyaligned and/or Taxonomy-eligible, the Group
voluntarily discloses the Adjusted EBITDA metric
as it provides coherence with other KPIs and
better reflects the extent to which the Group’s
growth is linked to Taxonomy-aligned and/or
Taxonomy-eligible activities. Adjusted EBITDA is
calculated based on the methodology determined
by the Group as it’s not part of the Taxonomy
Disclosures Delegated Act.
Taxonomy-eligible/aligned KPIs are calculated as
the KPIs associated to each specific Taxonomyeligible/aligned activity divided by the Group’s
total KPIs. While calculating the numerators,
KPIs were allocated to Taxonomy-eligible/
aligned activities based on the eligibility and the

alignment assessment described in the previous
paragraphs. The assumption was made that any
revenue, Adjusted EBITDA, Taxonomy OPEX, or
Taxonomy CAPEX that can be justifiably linked
to an identified Taxonomy-eligible/aligned activity
will be classified as Taxonomy-eligible/aligned
accordingly. Revenue and Adjusted EBITDA
KPIs are directly linked to the ratios used in the
Group’s Integrated Annual Report, whereas
Taxonomy OPEX and Taxonomy CAPEX refer
to the type of costs or additions required by the
Taxonomy Regulation. In the case of consolidated
EU Taxonomy figures, most consolidation
adjustments are made in line with the principles
used in the consolidated financial statements.
Double counting
All reported Taxonomy KPIs financial figures are
allocated directly or split using proxies into the
applicable Taxonomy-eligible/aligned activities
ensuring there is no double counting. The Group
considers that all its Taxonomy-eligible activities
contribute to climate change mitigation, therefore,
they are reported only under this objective.
Proxies
When financial numbers cannot be directly
allocated to a specific activity, proportional
accounting is applied using the most relevant
proxy based on the nature of the company
activities. Two distinct proxies are primarily used
for the indirect costs’ attribution. For energy
generating companies, allocation is based on
the quantities of electricity and/or heat generated
from different types of activities and sources. For
other Group companies, allocation is based on

employees’ working time dedicated to specific
activities. Planned, current, and/or historical data
is used, depending on availability and reliability.

or processes associated with Taxonomy-eligible/
aligned activities by the Group’s total Taxonomy
OPEX.

Calculation of Taxonomy-eligible/aligned
revenue

Taxonomy OPEX numerator includes operational
expenses related to repairs & maintenance
and short-term lease, whereas denominator
additionally includes IT maintenance costs.
Currently, the scope of OPEX included in the
Article 8 of the Disclosures Delegated Act is
open to interpretation, and there is a lack of
industry specific guidelines providing appropriate
inclusions, therefore, the Group calculated
Taxonomy OPEX based on the currently available
information. Where the operating expenses
were not material at the Group level, they may
have been excluded from the numerator, while
the total Taxonomy OPEX was included in the
denominator. An example of such exclusion could
be the Taxonomy OPEX related to administrative
buildings owned and used by the Group (7.7
Acquisition and ownership of buildings) as they
are often an integral part of generation units and
the significance of such expenses at the Group
level is low.

As defined in the Taxonomy Disclosures
Delegated Act, the share of the Group’s
Taxonomy-eligible/aligned revenue is calculated
by dividing the revenue derived from products
or services associated with Taxonomy-eligible/
aligned activities by the Group’s total revenue
(see ‘8.1 Consolidated statement of profit or loss').
Revenue associated with electricity generation
includes economic activities related to the
electricity generation from wind power,
hydropower, fossil gaseous fuels, electricity
generation using solar photovoltaic technology,
storage of electricity and cogeneration of heat/
cool and power from bioenergy. It also includes
revenue of balancing activities and/or hedging,
and/or regulatory activities, where the results
show figures that are not necessarily related
to electricity generation (for more information
on regulatory activities, see section ‘6.4
Governance’) but are directly related to or
necessary to perform Taxonomy-eligible/aligned
activities.

Taxonomy OPEX

dividing the Taxonomy OPEX related to assets

Group’s accounting systems and the uncertainties
mentioned above, there are temporary limitations
to the Taxonomy OPEX calculations, which
include the following:
– we cannot objectively evaluate the type of IT

maintenance costs that could be justifiably
included; thus, we use a conservative approach
and include all IT maintenance costs to the
denominator but do not include any costs to the
numerator;

– operational expenses related to the cost of

Calculation of Taxonomy-eligible/aligned
Taxonomy CAPEX
As defined in the Taxonomy Disclosures
Delegated Act, the share of the Group’s

combination’), '12 Property, plant and equipment'
(under ‘Additions’ and ‘Acquisition through
business combination’), '13 Right-of-use assets'
(under ‘Additions’)). Goodwill acquired through
business combinations was excluded from the
Taxonomy CAPEX KPI.

– if the asset has become operational during

the reported financial period, the Taxonomy
CAPEX related to expansion was reported as
Taxonomy-aligned;

– if the project was not completed in the year

– following the publication of Commission Notice

Changes in calculations
Following the annual review, several changes
were made to reflect more precise findings after
thorough analysis or to correct minor technical
errors. These adjustments, after recalculating the
2024 figures, allow for a more precise disclosure
of the EU Taxonomy KPIs:
– due to the different nature of the Group

company activities, two distinct proxies are
now used primarily for the indirect costs’
attribution. In 2024, the proxy primarily based
on employees’ working time dedicated to
specific activities was used;

– transport Repairs & Maintenance costs have

been included in both the numerator and
denominator for the 2024 and 2025 data;

– other minor changes involve a more precise

assessment of Taxonomy OPEX and
Taxonomy CAPEX inclusions and other
technical adjustments made to the 2024 and
2025 data, ensuring more accurate disclosure.

It should be noted that there are differences in
methodologies used to calculate Investments
and Taxonomy CAPEX (see the table on the
previous page). Total Investments reported by the
Group in 2025 were EUR 720.3 million, whereas
total Taxonomy CAPEX – EUR 966.5 million.

Contextual information about
Taxonomy Regulation KPIs
Revenue KPI
Taxonomy-eligible share of revenue in 2025 was
49.3% (or EUR 1,231.6 million) and increased by
3.4 pp compared to 2024, whereas Taxonomyaligned share of revenue was 40.2% (or EUR
1,005.0 million) and increased by 0.7 pp
compared to 2024.
The key drivers behind the increase in Taxonomyaligned share of revenue were:
– the increase in revenue of Taxonomy-aligned

activities, mainly in: i) revenue of storage
of electricity (EUR 56.8 million) due to new
services provided, ii) revenue of electricity
generation from wind power, cogeneration
of heat/cool and power from bioenergy and
electricity generation using solar photovoltaic
technology (EUR 53.0 million) due to new
assets launched;

– the increase was partly offset by electricity

generation from fossil gaseous fuels (EUR -80.6
million) driven by higher volumes generated
and new services provided and lower revenue
of electricity generation from hydropower (EUR
-29.3 million) mainly because of lower volumes
generated. The impact of electricity generation
from fossil gaseous fuels was also the main
difference between Taxonomy-eligible and
Taxonomy-aligned revenues.

Taxonomy-aligned revenue in 2025 consists only
of revenue from contracts with customers. In
2025, there were no significant amounts related
to Taxonomy-aligned activities pursued for the
Group’s own internal consumption.

Taxonomy CAPEX KPI

decreased by 6.0 pp compared to 2024.

Taxonomy-eligible share of Adjusted EBITDA
in 2025 was 88.5% (or EUR 483.5 million)
and increased by 8.6 pp compared to 2024.
Taxonomy-aligned share of Adjusted EBITDA
in 2025 was 81.4% (or EUR 444.6 million) and
increased by 9.8 pp compared to 2024.

Taxonomy-eligible share of Taxonomy CAPEX
in 2025 was 88.0% (or EUR 851.0 million)
and decreased by 5.3 pp compared to 2024.
Taxonomy-aligned share of Taxonomy CAPEX
in 2025 was 84.7% (or EUR 818.3 million) and
decreased by 8.0 pp compared to 2024.

– the decrease was partly offset by higher

In 2025, Taxonomy CAPEX considered as
Taxonomy-aligned in accordance with the
Taxonomy CAPEX plan was 75.4 million for
Electricity generation using solar photovoltaic
technology (4.1CCM), and EUR 53.9 million for
Storage of electricity (4.10CCM) activities. In
the period 2025–2028, the Taxonomy CAPEX
plan for these activities is expected to be
between EUR 0.3–0.4 billion. It is worth noting
that Taxonomy CAPEX plan does not include
potential future Investments for the expansion
of Taxonomy-aligned activities, that have not yet
been started but may or may not be started in the
future. Additionally, the actual Taxonomy CAPEX
amount incurred might differ from the estimate

provided for future periods in the Taxonomy
CAPEX plan due to external and internal factors
(including but not limited to, inflation, project
rescheduling, etc.). In addition, Taxonomy CAPEX
related to Taxonomy-aligned activities’ expansion
(4.1CCM, 4.3CCM, 4.10CCM), where the projects
did not have the FID made, were not included in
the Taxonomy CAPEX plan and the numerator
of Taxonomy CAPEX KPI, in 2025 amounted to
EUR 17.0 million (EUR 23.5 million in 2024).
Throughout the reporting period, the Group has
not issued new environmentally sustainable
bonds or debt securities with the purpose
of financing Taxonomy-aligned activities.
Nevertheless, it must be noted that the Group has
issued two green bonds in 2017 and 2018, where
part of the funds were used to finance Taxonomyaligned activities.

E4 Biodiversity
and
ecosystems

E4-1 Transition plan and consideration of
biodiversity and ecosystems in strategy and
business model

applies innovative approaches aimed at reducing
its environmental footprint and strengthening the
ecosystem's resilience.

Aligned with the Group’s strategy and objectives,
the Group is currently working on its biodiversity
transition plan, which will define actions and
targets within a comprehensive framework to
guide our approach through 2030. The plan will
include KPIs to drive measurable improvements
for both nature and business. It will be developed
in collaboration with biodiversity experts
and approved by the management to ensure
alignment with corporate sustainability targets.

ESRS 2 SBM-3 Material impacts, risks, and
opportunities and how they interact with the
Group’s strategy and business model.

This year, the Group conducted a GIS-based
assessment of its biodiversity footprint (not
publicly disclosed). The analysis covered physical
locations of our own operations, which allowed
us to identify our operational sites located
within or near sensitive biodiversity areas.
This assessment serves as a foundation for
further actions aimed at better understanding
of our impact on biodiversity, evaluating the
risks associated with the protection of natural
ecosystems, identifying priority areas where
mitigation or restoration measures need to be
implemented and tracking their progress.
To manage biodiversity-related risks and impacts,
the Group is taking steps to integrate biodiversity
and ecosystem considerations into its planning
and operational processes. The Group aims to
align projects with its sustainability objectives to
reduce environmental impacts and support their
long-term resilience. Stakeholders are proactively
engaged in planning and decision-making to
promote transparency and collaboration. Using
monitoring and evaluation data, the Group
continuously refines its practices to minimize
adverse effects. In addition, the Group seeks and

The table below provides descriptions of
our material IROs related to biodiversity and
ecosystems.
The material impact we have identified primarily
originates from: land acquisition or lease and
initial site preparation activities, which are
essential for green project development, but can

disrupt local ecosystems; the use of Kaunas
Lagoon's water for energy production at Kaunas
HPP and Kruonis PSHP (both Green Capacities),
which affect fish populations, waterbed structure,
and the sedimentation of organic matter;
deforestation and landscape changes, which
come from the necessity to cut down trees to
ensure the safety and resilience of power lines,
which can significantly affect ecosystems,
particularly in densely forested areas. The
material risk we have identified is linked to the
possible breach of environmental legislation or
environmental permits, including a significant
impact for energy production from wind due to the
protection of the rare species of birds. Both IROs
occur within our own operations.

ESRS 2 IRO-1 Description of the processes
to identify and assess material biodiversity
and ecosystem-related impacts, risks and
opportunities
The results of environmental monitoring programs
and the Environmental Investigation Agency
reports were used as a base when initiating
the double materiality assessment to identify
biodiversity related impacts. In addition, the Group
analysed its connections with nature using the
TNFD LEAP approach, including the identification
of sensitive areas and the assessment of impacts
and dependencies on ecosystem services. This
work was supported by GIS analysis of operational
sites and their proximity to protected areas and
other areas of high ecological value.
The Group collaborates with stakeholders,
including local communities and state institutions,
to identify and later implement practices that
mitigate the negative impacts on and the risks
related to biodiversity. The Group engages with the
affected communities through meetings, surveys,
and workshops, while incorporating their feedback
into the double materiality assessment. The
Group identifies sites, raw material production,
or sourcing activities that may have a negative
impact on biodiversity and ecosystems and
assesses relevant ecosystem services for affected
communities. Where impacts cannot be fully
avoided, mitigation measures are implemented
to maintain the value and functionality of priority
ecosystem services.

Corporate policies, implementation guidelines, frameworks and other documents
Title

Description

Applies to

The Group Environmental Policy
(available on our website)

The policy outlines a mitigation hierarchy principle with an objective to
minimize ecological consequences, protect valuable areas and species,
prevent deforestation, and consider local conditions in conservation efforts.
It also provides for restoration after our activities, ensuring environmental
benefits, sustainable resource management and avoiding the use of harmful
chemicals. The policy respects communities by outlining the informed
consent principle, prohibits trading in endangered species and promotes
ethical supplier practices.
The guidelines mandate regular impact assessments and apply the
principles of avoidance, minimization, restoration, and compensation during
infrastructure projects, preventing deforestation and supporting conservation
initiatives through collaboration with local communities and organisations.

E4-2 Policies related to biodiversity and
ecosystems
The Group aims to protect biodiversity
and ecosystems while reducing negative
environmental impacts and risks. All policies
related to biodiversity adhere to local and
European regulation. In the table on a previous
page are descriptions of the main policies,
guidelines or frameworks that govern our
material IROs.
Although there is no dedicated policy for tracing
all sourced products and materials that affect
biodiversity, the Group routinely gathers data
on the composition of key products, especially
those containing biological materials such as
paper, cardboard and wood. These are sourced
with recognised ecological certifications where
possible. This information supports strategic
planning to reduce resource consumption and
biodiversity impacts. For more details, see section
'E5 Resource Use and Circular Economy.’
E4-3 Actions and resources related to
biodiversity and ecosystems
The Group implements a range of actions to
avoid, reduce and manage its biodiversity and
ecosystem impacts across the project lifecycle.
These measures address the material negative
impact related to changes in the state and
condition of ecosystems and the material risk
of non-compliance with species protection

requirements, and are applied across planning,
construction, operation and decommissioning
stages.
Forest conservation and network infrastructure
efficiency improvement
The construction and maintenance of overhead
power lines interact with forested landscapes
and habitats. To minimise land use impacts,
vegetation disturbance and risks to species, ESO
(Networks) implements the following measures:
– In the most vulnerable areas, ESO (Networks)

is working to replace overhead power lines with
underground cables, minimizing their impact on
landscape and biodiversity. Between 2025 and
2028, there is a plan to replace 2,000 km of
overhead power lines in forested regions with
underground cables, with 365 km replaced in
2025. Following the installation of these cables,
protection zones will be reduced, enabling the
return of 3,950 hectares for forest expansion.
More information on cabling in the Networks
segment is available in section ‘E1-3 Actions
and resources in relation to climate change
policies’ and ‘S4-4 Taking action on material
impacts on consumers and end- users and
approaches to managing material risks and
pursuing material opportunities related to
consumers and end-users, and effectiveness
of those actions’.

Biodiversity in Group's wind and solar farms

– Protection zones around power lines are

periodically maintained to ensure safe, reliable,
and uninterrupted electricity supply, taking into
account local, protected, and invasive species.
During maintenance work, efforts are made to
minimize negative impacts on biodiversity by
responsibly removing hazardous trees, while
active cutting is limited during bird breeding
seasons. In the event of natural disasters,

222 / 451


=== pdf p.223 ===
Integrated Annual Report 2025 / Sustainability statement

damaged network repair work is carried
out, but efforts are made to avoid additional
negative impacts on ecosystems.
– During the maintenance and servicing of

overhead power lines, trees that pose a risk
to the electricity network are removed, and
regular vegetation management is conducted
within the power line protection zones.
Scientists from the Institute of Forestry have
developed recommendations and a decision
matrix to help identify which trees should be
subject to felling or pruning.

Bird protection and habitat restoration
measures
The Group takes targeted actions to manage
impacts on protected species, particularly birds
and bats, which are directly linked to the material
risk of non-compliance with environmental
requirements, and implements the following
measures:
– ESO (Networks) conducts the care and

dismantling of white stork nests only with
permission from the EPA. Measures are
being taken to install artificial nesting sites
after repairing the damage to the network
caused by naturally built nests. From 2021 to
2025, 474 nests were relocated or managed.
After the removal of nests or their remains,
compensatory measures are implemented
within 6 months by installing artificial nesting
sites in the immediate vicinity (no further than
100 meters from the removed nest). A registry
of restored nests is maintained, and reports are
submitted to the EPA twice a year.

– In summer 2025, Eurasian eagle-owls died

possibly due to electrical discharge from
utility poles in Šiauliai city. In response to

this incident, the Šiauliai city municipality,
together with ESO (Networks), the Ministry
of Environment, and the Ministry of Energy,
urgently addressed the bird protection issues.
During the project, ornithologists were
consulted, and special protective measures
were installed at critical utility poles to prevent
bird injuries while perching. These measures
are expected to prevent similar accidents in
the future and contribute to the conservation of
protected species. In 2026, a detailed study will
be conducted on bird protection in electricity
distribution networks. Contract signed with
the Nature Research Center. The study will
systematically analyse scientific literature on
the causes of bird mortality related to power
lines, identify sensitive bird species, classify
areas according to their sensitivity, and identify
the most dangerous sections of power lines.
In addition, the necessary bird protection
measures for overhead power lines will be
planned and a pilot classification of overhead
lines in western Lithuania will be carried out
according to the level of potential risk to birds.
The results of the study will be summarized
in a report, which will be coordinated with
the Ministry of the Environment and the
State Service for Protected Areas to ensure
its compliance with national environmental
standards and requirements.
– Ignitis Renewables (Green Capacities)

implements a wide range of biodiversity
protection and environmental monitoring
measures related to birds and other habitants
across its wind and solar projects in their
pre-construction, construction and postconstruction stages; the projects with initiatives
mentioned below represent only a part of the
broader portfolio:

Lithuania
– Birds and bats are being monitored one

year before the start of the construction of
wind farms in Pakruojis and Pasvalys. The
monitoring includes counting birds within a
2 km radius around the planned wind farms,
searching for nests of sensitive species in
forests, and observing migration in spring and
autumn. Bird colonies and feeding areas are
also being identified. MiniBat detectors are
used to monitor bats, recording their activity
and migration. Furthermore, the movement of
predatory birds is studied by attaching GPS
transmitters to assess their interaction with the
wind farm infrastructure. A monitoring program
has been prepared, covering three years
after the start of operations at Pakruojis and
Pasvalys wind farms.

– Kelmė wind farm is the first wind farm in

Lithuania to implement an advanced bird anticollision system ProTecBird, which detects
birds in real-time and automatically stops the
turbine, thereby protecting them from collisions.
This system was implemented to safeguard
birds flying throughout the wind farm. Also,
biodiversity management and action plans
were developed (available on our website).

– Birds and bats are being monitored at

Mažeikiai wind farm, the BIPS Irida system
has been installed at four turbines. Monitoring
programs for birds and bats are being prepared
for Jurbarkas, Kretinga, and Tauragė wind
farms.

Poland
– In the Silesia I and Silesia II wind farm projects

monitoring of birds and bats is currently being
conducted as part of the post-construction

phase. The monitoring started in 2024 and data
on collisions is being collected on a monthly
basis. In addition, a biodiversity management
plan has been commissioned for Silesia II
wind farm, which will be completed by the
end of next year. Environmental data is being
collected since August 2025.
Latvia and Estonia
– In our solar and wind projects: we are installing

bird perches for birds of prey at solar farms and
conducting bird and bat surveys before starting
the EIA for hybrid projects and wind farms.

Invasive plant control and ensuring
ecosystem stability
Invasive plants can degrade habitats and
outcompete native species. The Group
undertakes to control targeted invasive species in
order to enhance the ecosystem health, as shown
in the following examples:
– ESO (Networks) hires specialists to eradicate

Sosnowsky's hogweed, an invasive species
intolerable in Lithuania's green areas due
to its rapid spread and threat to both native
species and humans. Control measures
are being systematically and cooperatively
implemented to preserve ecosystem stability.
In 2025, actions were taken at the Musininkai,
Akmenėlė, Šilainiai, and Gižai technical
substations.

– In 2024, the Coastal Research and Planning

Institute prepared an invasive plant
management plan (not publicly available) for
Ignitis Renewables (Green Capacities) for the
Tauragė solar farm project, which includes
measures to protect the local ecosystem
and preserve biodiversity. In 2025, the

document was supplemented with specific
recommendations for the eradication of three
aggressively spreading goldenrod species:
Canadian (Solidago canadensis), giant (S.
gigantea), and tall (S. altissima), in order
to reduce their negative impact on natural

Flora and fauna protection measures
The Group implements targeted actions to
protect flora and fauna and applies the following
measures:
– Ignitis Renewables (Green Capacities) has

installed animal exit ramps in its solar farm
projects in Latvia, followed a meadow expert’s
opinion on lawn relocation, evaluated the
sites to check the current grass quality, made
plans for grass maintenance during the
operation and maintenance period as well
as implementing noise reduction measures.
In addition, individual landscape impact
reduction measures were implemented for
two neighbouring families, including the
construction of an embankment and planting
vegetation to block the view of the solar farm.

Protection of water ecosystems in
hydropower facilities
The Group prioritises the protection of aquatic
ecosystems by monitoring water level fluctuations
and implementing measures to safeguard fish
and bird populationsand applies the following
measures:
– The Nature Research Centre annually

evaluates the impact of water level fluctuations
on fish and water bird populations in the
Kaunas Lagoon from March to July. The
presentation/discussion of results takes
place with specialists from the Environmental

Protection Agency, the Environmental
Protection Department, and the State Service
for Protected Areas.
– Stationary pollution sources and their impact

on water quality are being monitored according
to the environmental monitoring program.

– The rules for the use and maintenance

of the Kaunas Lagoon are prepared in
accordance with the Description of the use
and maintenance of ponds and dammed lakes.
According to the rules, the Nature Research
Centre monitors water level fluctuations and
their impact on fish and water birds. These
services are provided under a contract. If
monitoring reveals that water level fluctuations
exceed 0.1 meters, compensation is calculated.
An exception was made for 2025–2026,
allowing the water level fluctuation limit to
increase to 0.4 meters per day. This exception
is necessary to ensure a sufficient balance of
market capacities for the country. To comply
with this requirement, an additional program
was prepared and coordinated with the
Environmental Protection Agency, called the
Kaunas Hydroelectric Reservoir Environmental
Conditions Study Program (hereinafter as the
Program), designed to assess the impact of
water level fluctuations on fish and water bird
populations. From 2027, the requirements will
return to the previous level, adhering to the
previously established water level fluctuation
standards. It is planned that the installation
of fish passes will have a positive impact
by facilitating fish migration upstream and
downstream, increasing fish biomass in the
Kaunas HPP reservoir and the Nemunas River
basin above the Kaunas HPP.

Biodiversity in Group's wind and solar farms

– Biodegradable oil is being used in Kaunas HPP

equipment that has direct contact with water.

Conducting environmental surveys for
offshore wind farm projects
To ensure sustainable offshore wind
development, the Group conducts environmental
impact assessments and applies the following
measures:
– In October 2025, the EIA report for

Lithuania’s first offshore wind farm project,
"Curonian Nord," was submitted for public and
transboundary consultations, as required by
national regulations and Espoo Convention. In
line with the Espoo Convention, transboundary
consultations were conducted with the Baltic
Sea countries, including Latvia, Estonia,
Finland, Sweden, Denmark, Germany, and
Poland. This phase of the national EIA
process marked a significant step in ensuring
transparency and public engagement in
decision-making. Public engagement was
integral to the process from the very beginning,
allowing for comments and suggestions,
reinforcing principles of environmental, social,
and economic responsibility. Following the
public consultations, the EIA report was revised
in accordance with the feedback received and
submitted for coordination to the EIA entities,
which include municipalities bordering the
Baltic Sea – Neringa, Klaipėda City, Palanga
City, Klaipėda District, also Kretinga District,
as well as authorities, responsible for public
health, cultural heritage, fire and rescue
services, protected areas, etc. After this
coordination phase, the EIA report will be
amended according to the comments received
and submitted to the responsible authority –
the Environmental Protection Agency. The
Environmental Protection Agency is expected
to make a decision regarding the project's
environmental impact in early 2026.

– In the Estonian offshore wind farm project, a

comprehensive set of environmental surveys
is currently underway, with final reports yet to
be completed. These include assessments of
marine processes and hydrodynamics, wind
and wave conditions, suspended sediment
transport, currents, ice conditions, and pollution
drift. Additional studies focus on seawater
quality, seabed biome and habitats (including
MBES and sampling), fish stock and fisheries
mapping (spawning areas and migration
routes), marine mammals, seabirds, migratory
birds, and bats. These surveys are essential for
evaluating potential environmental impacts and
ensuring the sustainable development of the
wind farm. The EIA programme for the offshore
wind farm and its electricity export cable was
approved by the authorities on 4 November,
2025, and we are now conducting the impact
assessment in accordance with the programme
(available on our website).

Assessing the environmental impact of
BESS projects
The Group evaluates the environmental impact
of energy storage systems to ensure minimal
disruption to biodiversity and local ecosystems
and implements the following measures:
– An environmental impact screening

assessment was conducted at Kelmė wind
farm, regarding the installation of BESS.
It was determined that there will be no
significant negative impact on biodiversity.
The infrastructure is designed to use as few
impervious surfaces as possible on which
BESS is installed. A noise assessment was
also carried out, during which the projected
noise dispersion indicators of the planned
economic activities and the battery equipment

were calculated. The assessment was divided
into four scenarios, considering different
levels of activity intensity and environmental
conditions.
– We plan to install BESS in the Kruonis PSHP

(Green Capacities) area, so an assessment of
the significance of the impact of its activities
on Natura 2000 sites was performed. The
responsible authority concluded that the
installation of such systems will not have a
significant impact on the Areas important
for habitat protection (AIHP) and Areas
important for bird conservation (AIBC) in the
Kaunas Lagoon, and the natural values will be
protected within them.

E4-4 Targets related to biodiversity and
ecosystems
Currently, the Group does not have specific
targets related to biodiversity and ecosystems,
but is enhancing its understanding of this topic,
analysing regulatory requirements, best practices
in the market and actively working towards
establishing comprehensive targets in the
near future.

Avoiding and/or mitigating impacts on the
state of species
The Group has identified that the construction
of wind farms and the operation of power grids
can negatively impact species' status and pose
a threat to protected bird species. This could
lead to the decline in their populations and the
degradation of ecosystems. As a result, there
is a risk of failing to comply with environmental
regulations.
The Group does not include biodiversity offsets
in its actions because no compensation targets
or key performance indicators have been
established, and data on the financing effects
(direct and indirect costs) of biodiversity offsets
has not been compiled due to limited availability.
Therefore, this aspect is currently not significant
to the Group's activities.

(available on our website)

The policy promotes rational and conservative management of resources, such as energy, fuel, commodities, waste, byproducts and other resources. It focuses on reducing waste from operations and ensuring safe and responsible resource
management based on pollution prevention principles. The Group applies the policy’s principles in its activities, ensuring that
resource efficiency is considered during the designing phase and environmental impacts are reduced based on the lifecycle
assessment. Its statements are in line with the global circular economy approach and guidelines.

E5-2 Actions and resources related to
resource use and circular economy
To implement the Group’s policies and the
Resource Use and Circularity Management
Guidelines, efforts were directed towards
enhancing the positive impact of waste-to-energy
(WtE) activities by diverting non-recyclable
waste from landfills and reducing the negative
impacts of waste generation and limited endof-life solutions. In 2025, the Group companies
advanced circularity by closing resource loops in
their operations, optimising the use of materials
and components and preparing for the end-of-life
of green energy projects.
Waste to energy
The WtE units in Vilnius and Kaunas (both Green
Capacities) enhance environmental sustainability
by converting non-recyclable waste into energy.
Economic growth, growth of consumption,
and urban development are driving the growth
of generated waste. In response, these units
offer a sustainable alternative to landfilling by
using unsortable waste as fuel for generating
electricity and district heating. They only accept
municipal waste that cannot be sorted or
recycled, thus complying with the permits for
integrated prevention and control of pollution
and following the waste hierarchy principle. To
promote effective waste management, facilities
carry out annual in-depth analyses of waste
composition and conduct daily visual inspections
to prevent unsuitable waste streams. The
activities of Kaunas and Vilnius CHPs (both
Green Capacities) are not treated as a separate
action to manage the impacts, but as daily
services the Group and its companies provide,
therefore, it is not included in the assessment of
significant investments and OPEX required for the
implementation of an action.

Resource optimisation
Kaunas CHP and Vilnius CHP (both Green
Capacities) optimise resource use by extending
the life of key components and reusing process
streams wherever feasible. Ultrafiltration and
excess pressure valve membranes are washed
and maintained rather than replaced. Cationic
loads are regenerated at sampling stations.
Condensate from the main process at the water
treatment plant is cleaned and reused, reducing
the need for fresh water and chemicals. The
companies collaborate with research institutions
to enhance material recovery and minimize
environmental impact. Their future plans include
closer collaboration with waste sorting and
recycling sectors, investments in advanced
technologies for flexible waste management, and
integration into the circular economy model. The
companies aim to optimise waste management by
investing in technologies to increase recyclable
material recovery before incineration and
focusing on education and cooperation with
municipalities and waste management companies
to promote sorting and recycling. They plan
to implement advanced monitoring systems
to better predict waste flows and optimise
incineration processes, reducing landfill waste
and maximizing energy potential.
Fly ash and bottom ash management
With increasing waste incineration volumes
at Vilnius and Kaunas CHPs (both Green
Capacities), the generation of hazardous fly
ash also rises. Due to its high concentrations
of dioxins, heavy metals, chlorine, and other
compounds, this waste cannot be disposed of
in landfills. Currently, it is being transported to
Langøya, an island in Norway, where advanced
technological processes transform the fly ash
into a gypsum-like material by mixing it with

acid and industrial wastewater. This material is
used to fill craters left by limestone extraction,
restoring sections of the island for public use.
As Langøya approaches its maximum capacity
as a result of receiving fly ash from most
European incinerators, the Group is actively
exploring alternative methods. This includes
utilising the hazardous fly ash in other products
by applying industrial symbiosis principles,
such as recovering salts and metals for reuse
in other industrial processes. By pursuing these
innovative approaches, the Group advances
circularity initiatives. Kaunas CHP and Vilnius
CHP (both Green Capacities) are deeply engaged
in these technologies and their development
and conduct feasibility studies to assess
their potential applications. Additionally, both
companies generate bottom ash and slag, which
are repurposed as secondary raw materials in
construction products for foundations and roads.
Waste prevention strategies
Waste prevention, guided by the waste hierarchy
principles, is a key priority in the Group
companies' waste management approach,
which aim to minimize the negative impact of
additional waste generation through educational
activities and responsible sourcing. To address
the negative impacts of waste generation, in 2025
the Group companies enhanced their responsible
sourcing strategies by focusing on avoiding
additional waste generation throughout the
Group's upstream value chain. ESO (Networks)
conducted a pilot project, incorporating new
circular economy procurement criteria aimed
at reducing GHG emissions through waste
prevention activities. Ignitis Renewables (Green
Capacities) completed an environmental impact
assessment for offshore wind farms, which will
inform the procurement of more sustainable
materials. For more information, see section ‘E4-

3 Actions and resources related to biodiversity
and ecosystems’. Ignitis (Customers & Solutions)
made economically and environmentally sound
decisions sound decisions by introducing
additional services for detecting equipment failure
and eliminating unreliable equipment, adapted to
evolving customer needs by efficiently upgrading
EV charging stations at certain locations where
initial ones proved inadequate, and will continue
to apply circularity criteria in equipment sourcing.
ESO (Networks), which is responsible for a
substantial portion of the generated waste
streams, delivers e-training courses and live
training sessions at waste storage sites to instruct
employees on waste reduction practices and
sorting techniques, thereby preventing waste and
diverting waste from disposal. We have plans
to extend these educational initiatives to the
contractors working at the Group’s premises or
on its projects. Moreover, the Group companies
show a mutual commitment to education as their
environmental experts are actively participating
in professional development events that focus
on waste prevention and advanced treatment
methodologies. These activities collectively
contribute to the overarching goal of waste
prevention and sustainable management of
waste.
Reuse, repair and maintenance
The Group companies place a strong focus on
maximizing the value of equipment and materials
through reuse, repair, and maintenance. ESO
(Networks) repurposes used electrical and
electronic equipment, as well as metal structures.
Collaborations with the Lithuanian Energy
Institute and metrological services facilitate
rigorous testing and calibration of natural gas
measurement instruments, thus enabling the
reuse of thousands of devices every year

231 / 451


=== pdf p.232 ===
Integrated Annual Report 2025 / Sustainability statement

and, in turn, reducing waste. The company
also systematically repurposes cardboard
packaging from smart metering devices by
shredding cardboard and using it as eco-friendly
package filler. At Elektrėnai Complex (Reserve
Capacities), components from old units are
being reincorporated into Units 7 and 8, where
feasible. Moreover, functional equipment of ESO
(Networks), Ignitis (Customers & Solutions) and
Vilnius Third Combined Heat and Power Plant
(CHP-3) (Reserve Capacities) was dispatched to
Ukraine to support the restoration of the country’s
critical energy infrastructure.
Ignitis (Customers & Solutions) extends the
lifespan of its equipment by repairing and reusing
it as well as employing preventive maintenance
and advanced monitoring algorithms. The
Ignitis ON charging EV network’s operation
and maintenance model, launched in 2025
across the Baltic countries, streamlines fault
management, enhances predictive maintenance,
and optimises resource efficiency through trend
analysis and proactive orders of spare parts.
When equipment fails outside warranty, we
make decisions to either repair it or dismantle
it for parts. Decommissioned EV chargers
are repurposed by reinstalling them, using
them for spare parts, or selling them, thus
supporting the circular economy principles.
Both Ignitis Renewables (Green Capacities)
and Ignitis (Customers & Solutions) maintain
strategic spare parts warehouses with plans to
expand them and improve resource efficiency,
thus facilitating a seamless transition towards
sustainable practices.

End-of-life solutions
Ignitis Renewables (Green Capacities)
has previously conducted a wind farm
decommissioning study to review the best
practices from across the globe. The study
examined various completed decommissioning
projects to identify the good practice examples.
The findings provide a basis for developing the
best practices for wind farm decommissioning in
the Baltic region and Poland.
At the end of life of a wind farm, solar farm
or BESS, the Group will make a decision on
whether to extend its lifecycle, repower, or to
decommission it. Insights and recommendations
from experts will help us identify optimal
strategies for the sustainable management of
the remaining waste. Ignitis Renewables (Green
Capacities) actively participates in an expert
working group at WindEurope and collects
the latest knowledge and the best practices
to inform its approach to end-of-life solutions.
Ignitis Renewables (Green Capacities) adheres
to industry guidelines and explores advanced
technologies for component recycling and
circular material recovery to ensure sustainable
and responsible project decommissioning in
the future.

E5-3 Targets related to resource use and
circular economy
The Group has not established formal Groupwide targets for resource use and the circular
economy but is committed to mitigating negative
impacts through its policies and actions. As
the Group enhances its understanding of these
areas and analyses regulatory requirements,
it is advancing towards defining effective
targets. To ensure these actions are consistent
with the Group's policies related to waste,
their effectiveness is being measured through
historical comparison of quantitative data on
waste treatment methods. Ultimately, these
targets will be designed to address the most
significant impacts and align with the Group's
policies related to the circular economy.

E5-5 Resource outflows
The Group is committed to enhancing
transparency in waste treatment data by
disclosing waste that has been either diverted
from disposal or directed to disposal, along with
detailed information on the methods used to treat
it. The data encompasses all identified waste
types generated by the Group’s operations and

projects. In 2025, findings revealed that waste
reclamation was the most prevalent treatment
method. The most significant reclaimed waste
streams included 105,824.2 tonnes of bottom ash
and slag, along with 17,562.3 tonnes of fly ash.
This represents a slight increase of 9.9% and
9.3% respectively compared to 2024. The rise in
waste volume is attributed to the higher volume of
non-recyclable waste being processed. Out of the

total waste generated, 145,379.3 tonnes (99.9%)
were recovered from disposal, with nearly all of it
(99.9%) effectively diverted from landfills. These
positive results highlight the Group's dedication
to sustainable waste management practices and
its commitment to achieving transparency and
efficiency in waste treatment.

Accounting policies
The Group's waste management accounting
policy complies with legal standards and
applies to all Group companies. It addresses
the waste generated during their operations
and projects, including electrical and electronic
waste, metal scrap, construction and plastic
waste, biodegradable waste (e.g., wood or
paper), waste from energy recovery processes,
and other types, including unsorted or mixed
categories. Data on these materials is primarily
recorded in national systems or gathered from
the Group’s contractors, along with evidence
collected directly from waste management
facilities, thus ensuring that the data is tracked
and evaluated comprehensively.
The methodology for calculating this data is
standardised, specifying whether it is obtained
from direct measurements or estimates, with
key assumptions clearly disclosed. The Group’s
waste Ttreatment methods adhere to standard
regulations, detailing the waste that is to be
diverted from or directed to disposal. The
Group follows the European Waste Catalogue
for waste descriptions, and its waste recovery
and disposal operations are guided by Annex
II and I to Directive 2008/98/EC (Waste
Framework Directive). This approach ensures
regulatory compliance and supports sustainable
management practices.
The Group does not use radioactive
components or products and therefore does not
generate radioactive waste.

The table on the side lists our material IROs
related to the health and safety of our own
employees. These IROs are connected to our

responsibility to promote safe working conditions,
perform oversight and trainings, raise awareness
and promote cooperation among employees. We

Work-related injuries and fatalities
Type: negative impact
Place in value chain: OO
Business segment: All
Changes compared to 2024: none

The energy sector involves working in high-risk
environment. That presents inherent occupational
health and safety risks, leading to health-related
impacts on our own workforce.

Occupational health and safety
Type: risk
Place in value chain: OO
Business segment: All

The energy sector involves working in high-risk
environment, such as construction sites, remote
locations, and in dangerous conditions (heights,
voltage, etc.). This can increase the risk of physical
harm, including accidents, injuries, and fatalities.

table in the next page provides descriptions
of the main policies, guidelines or frameworks
that govern our material IROs. The Group does
not have separate policies explicitly addressing

S1-1 Policies related to own workforce

S1-2 Processes for engaging with own
workforce and workers' representatives about
impacts

The Group aims to manage its IROs related to
health and safety in a structured manner via its
policies, standards or other frameworks. The

Health and safety related subjects are one of the
important topics discussed while engaging with
work councils and trade unions during collective

bargaining. The Group engages with its own
workforce according to the processes described
in the internal documents that align with ISO
45001. The Group companies without an ISO
45001 management system implement alternative
engagement processes, including recurrent
audits, project meetings, on-site support, toolbox
talks and communication, as well as monthly
meetings with the Group OHS team, where the
best practices are shared. The Group maintains
active dialogue with its employees about health
care, monitoring and maintaining a safe working
environment and improving health and safety
conditions at work. Workplace safety and health
risks are regularly assessed at the Group.

In each Group company, there is/are a person(s)
authorised by the employer, who is/are tasked
with implementing the requirements of OHS in
the company. Responsible persons are appointed
in accordance with both internal and external
legislation. The law stipulates the obligation to
have such authorized persons, and the Group's
internal regulations recommend that OHS
divisions report directly to the CEO.
The Occupational Safety, Health and
Environment function, which is managed by the
Group Head of Health, Safety and Environment
and regularly provides information to the parent
company’s Management Board, Sustainability

is responsible for the internal OHS regulations
issued by the Group, which apply to all Group

S1-3 Processes to remediate negative impacts
and channels for own workforce to raise
concerns
A mobile app ‘Not safe? Report!’ has been used
to help prevent health and safety incidents.
All employees are encouraged to report any
identified potential hazards. Each report is
reviewed and assessed by a designated member
of the Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) unit,
who initiates appropriate actions to eliminate the
hazard, depending on its nature. Employees who
submit such reports are rewarded with additional
benefits. A group-level OHS software is planned
to be fully implemented by end of 2026.
The Group is using a confidential reporting
platform, called Trust Line, enabling both internal
and external stakeholders to report potential or
actual OHS violations. For additional information,

see section ‘G1-1 Business conduct policies and
corporate culture’.
At the Group, all employees have access to
external, third-party mechanisms to address their
well-being and safety. If necessary, employees
can contact the State Labour Inspectorate, the
Fire and Rescue Department, the Ministry of
Energy, the National Energy Regulatory Council,
the National Crisis Management Centre, the
National Public Health Centre, and other relevant
authorities. These opportunities are available
to all employees, regardless of their job title or
position. They can also act through employee
representatives or other individuals who are
eligible to act on their behalf. Internally, the
Group provides a wellbeing mentors program,
i.e., a community of trained employees who
provide emotional support to their colleagues.
They talk with employees in person, run courses
and various team events. The Group offers
an emotional support line, a dedicated phone
number for employees and their family members
to receive confidential consultations with
experienced psychologists free of charge.
All Group employees are covered against
injuries or critical illnesses. In such events,
insurance benefits can be used to access better
rehabilitation services, purchase medicines or
medical supplies, or cover everyday needs. The
Personal Accident Insurance Memo for Ignitis
Group Employees (not publicly available) outlines
the scope of employee insurance coverage,
including insurance details and instructions how
to act, when an incident occurs.
S1-4 Taking action on material impacts on
own workforce, and approaches to managing
material risks and pursuing material
opportunities related to own workforce, and

effectiveness of those actions
The Group’s employees and their representatives
actively participate in the decision-making
process related to the design and implementation
of initiatives and processes aimed at improving
employee health, safety and wellbeing.
Vilnius CHP, Kaunas CHP and Ignitis Renewables
(all Green Capacities), Ignitis Gamyba (Reserve
Capacities and Green Capacities), ESO
(Networks), Ignitis (Customers & Solutions),
parent company and Ignitis Grupės Paslaugų
Centras, have OHS committees or work councils,
whose regulations define the role of employees
and their representatives in addressing health and
safety matters. Before implementing initiatives,
OHS representatives conduct consultations with
the relevant OHS committee to better understand
the needs and expectations of the workforce, if
needed. Additionally, these representatives hold
regular meetings, where committee members
can provide their opinions and suggestions
regarding the development and implementation
of initiatives. This collaboration ensures that the
measures the Group companies take are directly
aligned with the needs of the employees of the
Group and contribute to their wellbeing.
In line with the Group’s strategic management
principles, the Group companies are responsible
for preventing work-related traumas and illnesses,
ensuring safe workplace, complying with OHS
legislation and the policies’ principles and
ensuring that OHS responsibilities and objectives
are established at all levels.
The OHS objectives of the Group companies are
established in their strategic annual plans. The
Group companies carry out health inspections,
OHS training, ensure internal controls,

compliance with ISO 45001 and effective
occupational risk management. They also
encourage employee participation, support OHS
committees, foster safety culture through the ‘Not
safe? Report!’ app and prioritise data accuracy
and core values.
The Group identified an OHS risk during the
risk management process. The risk includes
workplace injuries and fatalities of workers
and contractors related to high-risk working
environment, inadequate social and cultural
context for preventing health and safety issues,
and failure to develop risk mitigation actions.
The risk is being mitigated using the following
continuous measures:
– employee training: the Group carries out

mandatory OHS training and certification of
employees as per legal requirements;

– contractor training: the Group trains and

educates contractors and calculates their TRIR;

– OHS control: companies, including contractors,

monitor OHS in workplaces;

– risk assessment: companies conduct and initiate

workplace risk assessments;

– incident sharing: companies share accident and

incident investigation findings with employees
and OHS specialists with the aim to prevent
them in the future;

– ISO 45001 certification: Ignitis Renewables

(Green Capacities), ESO (Networks), Ignitis
Gamyba (Reserve Capacities and Green
Capacities), Ignitis (Customers & Solutions) and
Ignitis Grupės Paslaugų Centras are ISO 45001
certified.

S1-5 Targets related to managing material
negative impacts, advancing positive
impacts, and managing material risks and
opportunities
Occupational health and safety is very important
to the Group, which is why the Group identified
work-related injuries and fatalities as a negative
impact and occupational health and safety as a
risk. In view of this, the following targets related to
the Group’s own workforce have been set in the
Group's Strategic Plan 2025–2028:
– zero fatal accidents;
– TRIR of employees is ≤1.0;
– TRIR of contractors is ≤1,7.

All strategic targets must be approved by the
Supervisory Board. The scope of TRIR reporting
includes all the workforce of the Group, including
employees and contractors. Employees are
regularly briefed about the TRIR status in periodic
meetings and other internal communications.
TRIR results are published in the Group's
Integrated Annual Reports. Employees were
indirectly involved in setting these targets by
participating in the maturity assessment of the
Group’s health and safety system.

Health and safety
The percentage of people in its own workforce who are
covered by health and safety management system (ISO
45001)
Number of fatalities in own workforce
Number of fatalities of other workers (contractors)

Lost Time Injury Rate (LTIR) is calculated as
the number of lost time injuries per one million
hours worked. The number of total annual
working hours for employees is recorded by
the Group’s internal personnel management
systems. LTIR includes the lost time injuries
that result in an incapacity for work for one or
more calendar days in addition to the day of the
incident.
TRIR is calculated in the same way as LTIR.
However, in addition to lost time injuries,
TRIR also includes the incidents after which
a person is able to perform work the day after
the incident, as well as the incidents where the
person has received medical treatment. For
contractors, the actual number of hours worked
is recorded based on the data provided by the
contractors.
Fatalities are the number of employees who lost
their lives as a result of a work-related incident.
Fatalities are included in both LTIR and TRIR.

Implementation guidelines, frameworks and documents
Title

Description

Applies to

The Group Remuneration
Policy
(available on our website)

The policy establishes clear and transparent remuneration principles and promotes employee motivation
while meeting shareholders’ expectations for sustainable development. It is designed to attract and retain
skilled, innovative, and globally minded employees. The key principles of this policy cover internal fairness,
external competitiveness, clarity, transparency, equal opportunities, and non-discrimination in regard to
remuneration.

All Group

The Group Code of Ethics
(available on our website)

The Group Code of Ethics defines the main principles and standards of a fair and transparent work
environment, including the following: ensuring equal employment opportunities and working conditions for
all individuals based solely on the nature of their professional activities; applying equal criteria and principles
when terminating an employment relationship; guaranteeing fair pay based on the functions performed,
the quality of work, professional and business abilities; and ensuring equal pay for equal work or work of
equal value. It ensures that the Group respects and protects human rights and freedoms, recognised in
national and international legislation, disseminates and fosters democratic values in accordance with the
guidelines set forth in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and International Labour Organisation
(ILO) Conventions No. 100, 111 and 155.

All Group

Directive (EU) 2022/2041
(available on website)

The Group follows the directive by ensuring that all its employees receive wages higher than the minimum.
Freedom of association and an obligation for employers to engage in collective bargaining and conclude
collective agreements are also ensured by complying by complying with applicable national labour laws in
each country of operation.

All Group

Internal Standard of
Additional Benefits

The eNPS survey is conducted quarterly across
the Group. All Group employees are invited
to participate in it. In the survey, employees
rate their agreement with the statement “I
would recommend my company as a potential
workplace to my friend or a good acquaintance”
on a scale of 1 to 10. The recommendation
index is calculated by subtracting the
percentage of employees who would not
recommend the employer (detractors) from the
percentage of those who would (promoters).

All employee data is collected from the Group's
personnel registration systems. The number
of employees was recorded at the end of
the financial year. The Group companies
also operate in Latvia, Estonia, Poland, and
Finland, but in these countries, the number of
employees does not represent >10% of the total
workforce of the Group. 95% of all employees
work in Lithuania.
In accordance with the Law on European Work
Councils of the Republic of Lithuania (IX-2031
Law on European Works Councils), the Group
did not meet the criteria of a community-scale
group of companies during the reporting period
and is therefore not obliged to initiate the
formation of a European Work Council.

The Group Equal Opportunities

The policy describes the main measures applied at the Group which are necessary for the implementation
of the equal opportunities and diversity principles. The Group has zero tolerance policy for any form of
discrimination, which includes direct and indirect discrimination, harassment, sexual harassment, or
instruction to discriminate on the basis of gender, race, nationality, ethnic origin, language, social status,
religion, faith, belief, convictions or views, age, sexual orientation, disability, state of health, family or marital
status, membership in a political party or association. According to the policy, employees' working conditions,
salary, additional benefits, and other aspects of their work in the organisation must be set in such a way
that helps create equal opportunities and helps employees to balance their work, private life, and familial
responsibilities.
The plan establishes the following commitments in respect to the specific groups of people who are
particularly sensitive: improving gender balance, creating inclusive environment for people with disabilities,
ensuring inclusion of people of all ages and raising awareness of LGBT inclusion.

All Group

to gender (including sexual harassment) or the threat thereof, is strictly prohibited. It also provides for
measures for employees who suffered abuse and harassment, who may contact the emotional support
line and receive a consultation from a psychologist as well as contact wellbeing mentors. In both cases
employees are guaranteed confidentiality.
The policy sets expectations for the management structure, organisational culture within the Group, ways
of attracting employees, employment relations, adaptation and career within the Group, including employee
education, upskilling as well as social dialogue.

Our commitment to talent development is
reinforced by the culture we are intentionally
building across the Group, guided by our four
core mindsets: United by Purpose, Owning
the Challenge, Pursuing Excellence, and
Passion for Reinvention. These mindsets
are embedded throughout the employee
lifecycle—from onboarding to development
and performance discussions—ensuring they
translate into everyday behaviors. Within our
performance management process, managers
and employees are encouraged to reflect on how
these mindsets are demonstrated in practice,
exchange constructive feedback, and agree on
actions to further strengthen these behaviors
where needed. In particular, Pursuing Excellence
drives our focus on delivering meaningful
impact and elevating the quality and value we
create for customers and society, while Passion
for Reinvention fosters continuous learning,
openness to new technologies, and a readiness
to innovate. By integrating these mindsets into
how we assess, develop, and support our people,
we cultivate a culture that enables innovation,
adaptability, and high performance—capabilities
essential for sustaining our competitive
advantage and achieving our strategic goals in
the energy transition.

A highly skilled workforce is crucial for achieving the
Group's strategic goals, especially as we navigate
the energy transition. New competencies are
essential for success in this evolving landscape,
and a lack of expertise may significantly impede
our progress. To maintain our competitive edge, we
must invest in talent development and cultivate a
culture that fosters innovation and excellence.

S2 Workers in
the value chain

ESRS 2 SBM-2 Interests and views of
stakeholders
Contractors are one of the key groups of
stakeholders in the Group’s value chain, playing
a crucial role in business development, and
supporting the overall strategic objectives of the
Group. Contractors were the key stakeholders
included in the dialogue to identity and validate
material impacts related to this standard. For
more on the interests and views of stakeholders,
see section ‘ESRS 2: SBM-2 Interests and views
of stakeholders’.

Sub-topic: Working conditions
Material IROs

Description

Work-related injuries and fatalities
Type: negative impact
Place in value chain: VC
Business segment: All
Changes compared to 2024: none

The energy sector involves working in high-risk
environment. That presents inherent occupational
health and safety risks, leading to health-related
impacts on workers in the value chain as our
contractors.

Occupational health and safety
Type: risk
Place in value chain: VC
Business segment: All
Changes compared to 2024: none

The energy sector involves working in high-risk
environment, such as construction sites, remote
locations, and dangerous conditions (heights,
voltage, etc.). This can increase the risk of physical
harm, including accidents, injuries, and fatalities.

ESRS 2 SBM-3 Material impacts, risks and
opportunities and how they interact with its
strategy and business model
While S1 focuses on the Group's own employees,
this section covers the equivalent impacts and
risks for workers in the value chain, including
contractors and suppliers.
The table on the side describes our material
IROs related to workers in the value chain. These
IROs are connected to our purpose to create
a green and secure energy as human capital
is a key resource for achieving it. It means that
we understand our responsibility to promote
safe working conditions, perform oversight and
conduct trainings, raise awareness, and promote
cooperation among the Group employees and
contractors while improving OHS management,
procedures, and communication within and
outside the Group. These IROs are linked to
us through our own operations and through our
relationships with contractors.
At this stage, the Group is unable to include the
full scope of its value chain workers due to limited
access to necessary and reliable information.
Our focus has been on first-tier suppliers and

contractors, and we have identified material
IROs within this scope. On the other hand, the
Group has considered issues of child labour or
forced labour, but no significant IROs have been
identified related to these topics. No regions
or specific countries have been identified as
particularly significant for these IROs.
S2-1 Policies related to value chain workers
The Group aims to manage its IROs related to
workers in the value chain in a structured manner
via its policies or other frameworks. The table in
the next page provides descriptions of the main
policies, guidelines or frameworks that govern our
material IROs.
S2-2 Processes for engaging with value chain
workers about impacts
The Group’s engagement strategy unfolds in
multiple stages of the supply chain procedures.
It begins with the selection of suppliers, followed

by the contract signing stage, where suppliers
are required to accept the SCE requirements.
This is followed by engagement through
various channels, ongoing SCE monitoring, and
inspections to assess the adherence to the OHS
requirements, with the primary focus on safety,
which must be maintained until the final contract
stage. This structured engagement enables the
Group to maintain consistent oversight over the
needs of the Group’s suppliers.
The Group interacts with value chain workers
directly by awarding procurement contracts
through one of its companies. After the Group
company signs a procurement contract with a
supplier, each contract is designated a contract
owner, an employee of the Group company, who
is assigned to ensure the proper performance
of the contract. The contract owner collaborates
with the supplier, providing feedback on contract
performance, clarifying information, and
responding to any inquires.

Implementation guidelines, frameworks and documents
Title

Description

Applies to

The Group
Occupational
Health and Safety
Policy
(available on our
website)

The policy is intended to ensure that workers throughout
the value chain adhere to the same OHS standards as the
Group's own employees. It emphasises the selection of
reliable partners who prioritise safety and comply with OHS
requirements, thereby minimising the risks and reducing
the negative impact related to work-related injuries and
fatalities. Under the policy, contractors must comply with
all OHS requirements of the Group, including carrying out
relevant occupational risk assessments, training, reporting
incidents, and observing processes. The Group companies
are responsible for ensuring contractors’ compliance with
the policy through prequalification, onboarding, and active
monitoring.

All Group

The SCE comprehensively covers the entire supply chain. It
applies to all suppliers and business partners involved in the
Group's supply chain and outlines their obligation to provide
a safe and healthy working environment for all employees. In
accordance with the SCE, robust frameworks for occupational
health and safety governance are expected to be established
to ensure compliance with relevant laws, regulations, and
customer requirements, as well as effectively manage
operational hazards and risks associated with their operations.
The SCE addresses potential risks related to labour practices
in accordance with the principles set forth in the UDHR, the
ILO’s Convention on Fundamental Principles and Rights at
Work, and the United Nations Global Compact (UNGC).

All Group

The Group has established regulations, which are adopted
by all Group companies, to guide the work of contractors
and ensure that all personnel, including dispatched staff,
contractors, and other external entities, comply with work and
safety requirements. The issues related to high-risk suppliers
are also addressed by requiring additional instructions or
training for certain high-risk tasks, including such instructions
or training for the Group’s own employees. Furthermore,
instructions may vary depending on the nature of the work
environment, such as remote locations or the Group company
premises.

Ignitis
Renewables,
Ignitis Gamyba,
Kaunas and
Vilnius CHPs (all
Green Capacities),
ESO (Networks)

The Group
Supplier Code of

Company specific
internal standards
and instructions
(not publicly
available)

Prior to signing the contract, the supplier’s
representative is introduced to and must consent
to the Group’s policies, including the SCE.
The Group company then cooperates with the
supplier's representative and its employees prior
to and during the procurement contract period.
If concerns arise, suppliers can disclose their
inquires at any time by contacting the Group
company’s representative. The frequency of
cooperation depends on each procurement
contract signed between the Group company and
the supplier. The Group company’s dedicated
staff monitors the progress of contract work,
liaising with contractors, providing feedback and
visiting sites to assess contractors' health and
safety performance. To achieve the best results,
the Group has initiated various engagement
methods, such as sending newsletters to its
suppliers, holding quarterly meetings between
HSE personnel and contractors' representatives,
organising toolbox talks, and hosting contractor
safety days.
To evaluate the effectiveness of its engagement,
the Group monitors the outcomes of its activities
and relies on improvements in key performance
indicators. These improvements are intended
to ultimately contribute to the goal of decent
work and economic growth as outlined in the
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
TRIR results along with assessments of suppliers
on their adherence to the SCE are further
discussed in section S2-4. The Group Head of
Health, Safety and Environment is responsible
for overseeing the TRIR results, while supplier
engagement is managed by the Head of Group
Procurement.
Direct engagement with value chain workers or
their legitimate representatives is recognised as

the most effective approach for addressing labour
and health and safety issues, as it facilitates
open communication, a better understanding
of concerns, and the development of more
effective solutions. Accordingly, the Group
intends to maintain structured engagement and,
in the upcoming year, strengthen collaboration
with contractors to increase their engagement,
education while sharing the best practices.
The Group acknowledges the importance of
understanding the perspectives of vulnerable and
marginalized workers within the value chain, such
as migrant workers. However, there is currently
no dedicated procedure in place to ensure their
specific perspectives are addressed. Meanwhile,
the Group’s contractors follow national laws that
protect vulnerable workers, ensuring that their
rights and wellbeing are upheld in accordance
with legal standards.

For additional information, see section ‘G1-1
